units.title: Clinical decision-making
units.summary: A great deal of knowledge and skill is required to practise as a doctor. Physicians in the 21st century need to have a comprehensive knowledge of basic and clinical sciences, have good communication skills, be able to perform procedures, work effectively in a team and demonstrate pro-fessional and ethical behaviour. But how doctors think, reason and make decisions is arguably their most critical skill. Knowledge is necessary, but not sufficient on its own for good performance and safe care. It is estimated that diagnosis is wrong 10%–15% of the time in specialties such as emergency medicine, internal medicine and general practice.

units.title: The problem of diagnostic error
units.summary: It is estimated that diagnosis is wrong 10%–15% of the time in specialties such as emergency medicine, internal medicine and general practice. Diagnostic error is the most common, costly and dangerous of medical mistakes and much of it is preventable. For every diagnostic error there are usually several root causes. Studies identify three main categories, shown in Box 1.1.

units.title: Clinical reasoning: definitions
units.summary: ‘Clinical reasoning’ describes the thinking and decision-making pro-cesses associated with clinical practice. Our understanding of clinical reasoning derives from the fields of education, cognitive psychology, studies of expertise, and the diagnostic error and health systems literature. For novices, clinical reasoning can be conceptualised as a process with different components, each requiring specific knowledge, skills and behaviours. units.title: Evidence-based history and physical examination
units.summary: Even with major advances in medical technology, the history remains the most important part of the clinical decision-making process. Studies show that physicians make a diagnosis in 70%–90% of cases from the history alone. It is important to remember that the history is explored not only with the patient, but, if necessary, from all available sources (with consent if required): for example, paramedic and emergency department notes, eye-witnesses, relatives and/or carers. Clinicians also need to be aware of the diagnostic usefulness of clinical features in the history and physical examination.

units.title: Sensitivity and specificity
section_path: Use and interpretation of diagnostic tests
units.summary: Diagnostic tests have characteristics termed ‘sensitivity’ and ‘specificity’. Sensitivity is the ability to detect true positives; specificity is the ability to detect true negatives. Even a very good test, with 95% sensitivity, will miss 1 in 20 people with the disease. Every test generates ‘false posi-tives’ and ‘false negatives’ (Box 1.4).

units.title: Prevalence of disease
section_path: Use and interpretation of diagnostic tests
units.summary: Consider this problem that was posed to a group of Harvard doctors. The problem originates from a 1978 article in the New England Journal of Medicine (Casscells et al, see ‘Further information’): if a test to detect a disease whose prevalence is 1:1000 has a false-positive rate of 5%, what is the chance that a person found to have a positive result actually has the disease, assuming you know nothing about the person’s symp-toms and signs? Assume the test generates no false negatives and take a moment to work this out. In this problem, we have removed clinical probability and are only considering prevalence.

units.title: Dealing with uncertainty
section_path: Use and interpretation of diagnostic tests
units.summary: Clinical findings are imperfect and diagnostic tests are imperfect. It is important to recognise that clinicians frequently deal with uncertainty. By expressing uncertainty as probability, new information from diagnostic tests can be incorporated more accurately. However, subjective esti-mates of probability can sometimes be unreliable.

units.title: Problem representation
units.summary: Many students are taught to formulate a differential diagnosis after the history, physical examination and initial test results, but the ability to accurately articulate a ‘problem representation’ first and then con-struct a prioritised differential diagnosis based on this, including relevant ‘must-not-miss’ diagnoses, is a key step in the clinical reasoning pro-cess. Problem representation refers to how information about a prob-lem is mentally organised. Studies show that expert clinicians spend far more time on defining and representing a problem before trying to solve it compared with novices, and novices are more likely to be unsuccessful in solving a problem because they have not accurately represented the problem in the first place. The ability to synthesise all the available infor-mation and encapsulate it into a problem representation using precise medical language is an important skill that needs to be learned.

units.title: Clinical reasoning concepts
units.summary: Decades of studies in cognitive psychology and, more recently, func-tional magnetic resonance imaging demonstrate two distinct types of processes when it comes to decision-making: humans have a fast, intu-itive, pattern-recognising way of thinking which uses little cognitive effort (known as type 1 thinking) and a more deliberate, analytical one which engages our working memory (known as type 2 thinking). This is known as ‘dual process theory’ and Box 1.6 explains this in more detail. Psychologists estimate that we spend 95% of our daily lives engaged in type 1 thinking – the intuitive, fast, subconscious mode of decision-mak-ing. Imagine driving a car, for example: it would be impossible to function efficiently if every decision and movement were as deliberate, conscious, slow and effortful as in our first driving lesson. Figure 1.6 illustrates the common cognitive biases prevalent in medical practice.

units.title: Common cognitive biases in medicine
units.summary: Figure 1.6 illustrates the common cognitive biases prevalent in medical practice. Biases often work together; for example, in overconfidence bias (the tendency to believe we know more than we actually do), too much faith is placed in opinion instead of gathered evidence. This bias can be augmented by availability bias and finally by commission bias (the ten-dency towards action rather than inaction) – sometimes with disastrous results. The mark of a well-calibrated thinker is the ability to recognise what mode of thinking is being employed and to anticipate and recognise situ-ations in which cognitive biases and errors are more likely to occur.

units.title: Thinking about thinking
units.summary: Research has highlighted the importance of being aware of and being able to think about one’s own thinking (also known as metacognition). Several studies have demonstrated that engaging in reflection during diagnostic decision-making improves performance (Prakash et al, see ‘Further information’). This can be as simple as asking, ‘What is the evi-dence for this diagnosis? What else could it be?’ Reflection is most effec-tive when the case is more complex (relative to the clinician).

units.title: Shared decision-making
units.summary: ‘Patient-centred evidence-based medicine’ refers to the application of best available research evidence while taking individual patient factors into account; these include both clinical and non-clinical factors (e.g. the patient’s social circumstances, values and wishes). For example, a 95-year-old man with dementia and a recent gastrointestinal bleed is admitted with an inferior myocardial infarction. Should he be treated with dual antiplatelet therapy and low-molecular-weight heparin as recommended in clinical guidelines for myocardial infarction? Realistic medicine is a movement that started in Scotland (see ‘Further information’) with the aim of empowering patients and their families to discuss their tests and treatment, including any side effects and poten-tially negative outcomes, and whether they need a test or treatment at all.

units.title: Red flags and ROWS (‘rule out worst-case scenario’)
section_path: Red flags and ROWS (‘rule out worst-case scenario’)
units.summary: These are strategies that force doctors to consider serious diseases that can present with common symptoms. Red flags in back pain are listed in Box 25.19. Considering and investigating for possible pulmonary embo-lism in patients who present with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness is a common example of ruling out a worst-case scenario, as pulmonary embolism can be fatal if missed. Red flags and ROWS help to avoid cognitive biases such as the ‘framing effect’ and ‘premature closure’.

units.title: Cognitive biases
section_path: Clinical decision-making: putting it all together
units.summary: Imagine during this case that the patient had been handed over to you as ‘nothing wrong – probably a pulled muscle’. Cognitive biases (our subconscious tendencies to respond in a certain way) would come into play, such as the ‘framing effect’, ‘confirmation bias’ and ‘search satis-ficing’. The normal clinical examination might confirm the diagnosis of musculoskeletal pain in your mind, despite the examination being entirely consistent with pulmonary embolism and despite the lack of history and examination findings (e.g. chest wall tenderness) to support the diagno-sis of musculoskeletal chest pain.

units.title: Answers to problems
units.summary: Almost half of doctors surveyed said 95%, but they neglected to take prevalence into account. If 1000 people are tested, there will be 51 posi-tive results: 50 false positives and 1 true positive. The chance that a per-son found to have a positive result actually has the disease is therefore only 1/51 or ~2%. This puzzle is from the book Thinking, Fast and Slow, by Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman (see ‘Further information’). The distinctive mark of this easy puzzle is that it evokes an answer that is intuitive, appealing – and wrong.

units.title: Clinical therapeutics and good prescribing
units.summary: Modern drugs are usually discovered by screening compounds for activ-ity either to stimulate or to block the function of a specific molecular tar-get, which is predicted to have a beneficial effect in a particular disease (Box 2.2). Examples are des-ferrioxamine, a chelator used in the treatment of iron overload; mannitol, an osmotic agent used for cerebral oedema; and general anaesthetics, which work by altering the biophysical properties of lipid membranes. The following characteristics of the interaction of drugs with receptors illustrate some of the important determinants of the effects of drugs: • Affinity describes the propensity for a drug to bind to a receptor and is related to the ‘molecular fit’ and the strength of the chemi-cal bond. Understanding what the body does to the drug (Fig. 2.3) is extremely important for prescribers because this forms the basis on which the optimal route of administration and dose regimen are chosen and explains the majority of inter-individual variation in the response to drug therapy.

units.title: Inter-individual variation in drug responses
units.summary: Prescribers have numerous sources of guidance about how to use drugs for many conditions. However, this advice is based on average dose– response data derived from observations in many individuals. When applying this information to an individual patient, prescribers must take account of inter-individual variability in response. Some of this variability is predictable and good prescribers are able to anticipate it and adjust their prescriptions accordingly to maximise the chances of benefit and minimise harm.

units.title: Adverse outcomes of drug therapy
units.summary: Some important definitions for the adverse effects of drugs are: A harmful event that occurs while a patient is taking a drug, irrespective of whether the drug is suspected of being the cause. An unwanted or harmful reaction that is experienced following the administration of a drug or combination of drugs under normal conditions of use and is suspected to be related to the drug. An ADR will usually require the drug to be dis-continued or the dose reduced. A drug interaction has occurred when the administration of one drug increases or decreases the beneficial or adverse responses to another drug. Although the number of potential interacting drug com-binations is very large, only a small number are common in clinical practice.

units.title: Drug interactions
units.summary: A drug interaction has occurred when the administration of one drug increases or decreases the beneficial or adverse responses to another drug. Although the number of potential interacting drug com-binations is very large, only a small number are common in clinical practice. Important drug interactions are most likely to occur when the affected drug has a low therapeutic index, steep dose–response curve, high first-pass or saturable metabolism, or a single mechanism of elimination. Pharmacodynamic interactions occur when two drugs produce additive, synergistic or antagonistic effects at the same drug target or physiologi-cal system.

units.title: Medication errors
units.summary: A medication error is any preventable event that may lead to inappro-priate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in the control of the health-care professional or patient. Errors may occur in prescribing, dispensing, preparing solutions, administration or monitor-ing. Many ADRs are considered in retrospect to have been avoidable with more care or forethought; in other words, an adverse event con-sidered by one prescriber to be an unfortunate ADR might be consid-ered by another to be a prescribing error. Several thousand medication orders are dispensed and administered each day in a medium-sized hospital.

units.title: Drug regulation and management
units.summary: Naturally occurring products have been used to treat illnesses for thou-sands of years and some remain in common use today. Examples include morphine from the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) and dig-italis from the foxglove (Digitalis purpurea). Although plants and animals remain a source of discovery, the majority of new drugs come from drug discovery programmes that aim to identify small-molecule compounds with specific interactions with a molecular target that will induce a pre-dicted biological effect. The usual pathway for development of these small molecules includes: identifying a plausible molecular target by investigating path-ways in disease; screening a large library of compounds for those that interact with the molecular target in vitro; conducting extensive medic-inal chemistry to optimise the properties of lead compounds; testing efficacy and toxicity of these compounds in vitro and in animals; and undertaking a clinical development programme (Box 2.16). Many medicines meet the three key regulatory requirements of quality, safety and efficacy.

units.title: Managing the use of medicines
units.summary: Many medicines meet the three key regulatory requirements of quality, safety and efficacy. Although prescribers are legally entitled to prescribe any of them, it is desirable to limit the choice so that treatments for spe-cific diseases can be focused on the most effective and cost-effective options, prescribers (and patients) gain familiarity with a smaller number of medicines, and pharmacies can concentrate stocks on them. The process of ensuring optimal use of available medicines is known as medicines management or quality use of medicines. It involves care-ful evaluation of the evidence for benefit and harm, an assessment of cost-effectiveness and support for processes to implement the resulting recommendations.

units.title: Prescribing in practice
units.summary: Prescribing should be based on a rational approach to a series of chal-lenges (see Box 2.1). Ideally, prescribing should be based on a confirmed diagnosis but, in reality, many prescriptions are based on the balance of probability, taking into account the most likely differential diagnosis. The goals of treatment are usually clear, particularly when relieving symp-toms such as pain or nausea. Sometimes the goal of treatment is to prevent future events, such as the use of bisphosphonates to prevent fractures. The aim of monitoring drug therapy is to inform decisions about dose titration (up or down), discontinuation or substitution of treatment.

units.title: Monitoring drug therapy
units.summary: The aim of monitoring drug therapy is to inform decisions about dose titration (up or down), discontinuation or substitution of treatment. Monitoring can be achieved subjectively by asking the patient about symptoms or by measuring a clinical effect, on clinical examination, such as extent of an eczematous rash or joint swelling, physiological measure-ments, like assessment of blood pressure, and pulse oximetry, imaging or by laboratory tests. If the pharmacodynamic effects of the drug are difficult to assess using the above approaches, the plasma drug con-centration may be measured if this is closely related to the effect of the drug (see Fig. Rational prescribing ultimately rests on continuous monitoring of the balance between the risks and benefits of drug therapy.

units.title: Clinical genetics
units.summary: Genes are functional units encoded in double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), packaged as chromosomes and located in the nucleus of the cell: a membrane-bound compartment found in all cells except erythro-cytes and platelets (Fig. DNA consists of a linear sequence of four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), thymine (T) and guanine (G). It forms a ‘double helix’, a twisted ladder-like structure formed from two comple-mentary strands of DNA joined by hydrogen bonds between bases on the opposite strand. These bonds can form only between a C and a G base or an A and a T base. Genes are functional elements within the chromosome that are capable of transmitting information from the DNA template via the production of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) to the production of proteins.

units.title: From DNA to protein
units.summary: Genes are functional elements within the chromosome that are capable of transmitting information from the DNA template via the production of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) to the production of proteins. The human genome contains over 20 000 genes, although many of these are inactive or silenced in different cell types, reflecting the variable gene expression responsible for cell-specific characteristics. Gene expression in its sim-plest sense means that a gene produces a corresponding protein.

units.title: Non-coding RNA
units.summary: Approximately 4500 genes in humans encode non-coding RNAs (ncR-NAs) rather than proteins. There are various categories of ncRNA, including transfer RNA (tRNA), ribosomal RNA (rRNA), ribozymes and microRNA (miRNA). The miRNAs, which number over 1000, have a role in post-translational gene expression: they bind to mRNAs, typically in the 3′UTR, promoting target mRNA degradation and gene silencing. Together, miRNAs affect over half of all human genes and have important roles in normal development, cancer and common degenerative disor-ders.

units.title: Cell death, apoptosis and senescence
units.summary: With the exception of stem cells, human cells have only a limited capacity for cell division. The Hayflick limit (named after the anatomist who discov-ered this) is the number of divisions a cell population can go through in culture before division stops and enters a state known as senescence. Senescence is a potent anti-tumour mechanism since it prevents abnor-mal cells from replicating; however, senescent cells are not dead and may persist until they are removed by immune processes. If their presence is prolonged, they may have a deleterious effect on tissues.

units.title: Genomics health and disease
units.summary: There are many different classes of variation in the human genome, cat-egorised by the size of the DNA segment involved and/or by the mecha-nism giving rise to the variation. Nucleotide substitutions, insertions and deletions The substitution of one nucleotide for another is the most common type of genomic variation. This is caused by misincorporation of a nucleotide during DNA synthesis or by chemical modification of the base. The consequence of an individual genomic variant depends on many factors, including the variant type, the nature of the gene product and the position of the variant in the protein. Variants can have profound or subtle effects on gene and cell function.

units.title: Consequences of genomic variation

units.title: Normal genomic variation
units.summary: We each have 3–5 million variants in our genome, occurring approxi-mately every 300 bases. These variants are mostly polymorphisms, aris-ing in more than 1% of the population; they have no or subtle effects on gene and cell function and are not associated with an increased risk of disease. Polymorphisms can occur within exons, introns or the intergenic regions that comprise 98%–99% of the human genome. The most frequent variants are single nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNP (pronounced ‘snip’), describing the substitution of a single base.

units.title: Familial genetic disease
units.summary: Familial genetic disease, also known as monogenic disease, is caused by constitutional variants which are inherited through the germline. It has been estimated that about 1% of the human population carries constitu-tional variants that are pathogenic and can directly cause disease or play a major role in the pathogenesis of disease. It should be noted that different pathogenic variants can have differ-ent consequences, depending on the genetic mechanism underlying the disease. The variants that cause familial genetic disease can also vary in penetrance.

units.title: Somatic genetic disease

This influences hormone regulation and many other cell functions, resulting in focal lesions in the skeleton and endocrine dysfunction. units.title: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies
units.summary: For decades, the analysis of metaphase chromosomes by light micros-copy was the mainstay of clinical cytogenetic analysis, the aim being to detect gains or losses of whole chromosomes (aneuploidy) or large chromosomal segments (> 4 million bp). More recently, genome-wide microarrays (array comparative genomic hybridisation or array CGH and SNP arrays) have replaced chromosome analysis, allowing rapid and precise detection of segmental gain or loss of DNA throughout the genome (see Box 3.3). Microarrays consist of grids of multiple wells containing short DNA sequences (reference DNA) that are complemen-tary to known sequences in the genome. In array CGH, patient and reference DNA are each labelled with a coloured fluorescent dye (gen-erally, patient DNA is labelled with a green fluorescent dye and refer-ence DNA with a red fluorescent dye) and added to the microarray grid. units.title: Looking at genes
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies
units.summary: Gene amplification: polymerase chain reaction The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a fundamental laboratory tech-nique that amplifies targeted sections of the human genome for further analysis – most commonly, DNA sequencing. The method uses thermal cycling: repeated cycles of heating and cooling allow the initial separation of double-stranded DNA into two single strands (known as denaturation) followed by DNA amplification, using DNA polymerase (under cooled conditions). Since DNA polymerase is only able to add a nucleotide to an existing 3′OH group, specially designed primers (short segments of nucleotides) are used to anneal to the DNA template and target the region for amplification.

units.summary: Genomics in rare neurodevelopmental disorders Although, by definition, the diagnosis of a rare disorder is made infre-quently, rare diseases collectively affect about 3 million (1 in 17) peo-ple in the UK, the majority of whom are children. NGS has transformed the ability to diagnose individuals affected by a rare disease. Whereas previously, when we were restricted to the sequential analysis of single genes, a clinician would need to make a clinical diagnosis in order to target testing, NGS instead allows the interrogation of multiple genes in a single experiment. units.title: Treatment of genetic disease
units.summary: Pharmacogenomics is the science of dissecting the genetic determi-nants of drug kinetics and effects using information from the human genome. For more than 50 years it has been appreciated that polymor-phic variants within genes can affect individual responses to some drugs. For example, loss-of-function variants in a gene called CYP2D6 pres-ent in 3% of the population cause hypersensitivity to debrisoquine, an adrenergic-blocking medication formerly used for the treatment of hyper-tension. This gene is part of a large family of highly polymorphic genes encoding cytochrome P450 proteins, mostly expressed in the liver, which determine the metabolism of a host of specific drugs.

units.title: Ethics in a genomic age
units.summary: As genomic technology is increasingly moving into mainstream clinical practice, it is essential for clinicians from all specialties to appreciate the complexities of genetic testing and consider whether genetic testing is the right thing to do in a given clinical scenario. To exemplify the ethical considerations associated with genetic testing, it may be helpful to think about them in the context of a clinical scenario. As you read the scenario, try to think what counselling/ethical issues might arise: A 32-year-old woman is referred to discuss BRCA2 testing; she is currently pregnant with her second child (she already has a 2-year-old daughter) and has an identical twin sister. Her mother, a healthy 65-year-old with Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, participated in direct-to-consumer (DTC) testing for ‘a bit of fun’ and a BRCA2 gene variant – common in the Ashkenazi Jewish population – was identified.

units.title: The inflammatory response
units.summary: Inflammation is the response of tissues to injury or infection and is necessary for normal repair and healing. This section focuses on the general principles of the inflammatory response and its multisystem manifestations. The role of inflammation in specific diseases is discussed in many other chapters of this book.

units.title: Acute inflammation
units.summary: Acute inflammation is the result of rapid and complex interplay between the cells and soluble molecules of the innate immune system. The clas-sical external signs include heat, redness, pain and swelling (Fig. The inflammatory process is initiated by local tissue injury or infection. Damaged epithelial cells produce cytokines and antimicrobial peptides, causing early infiltration of phagocytic cells.

units.title: Chronic inflammation
units.summary: In most instances, the development of an active immune response results in clearance and control of the inflammatory stimulus and resolution of tissue damage. Failure of this process may result in chronic inflammation, with significant associated bystander damage, known as hypersensitivity responses. Persistence of microorganisms can result in ongoing accumu-lation of neutrophils, macrophages and activated T lymphocytes within the lesion. If this is associated with local deposition of fibrous tissue, a granuloma may form.

units.title: Laboratory features of inflammation
units.summary: Inflammation is associated with changes in many laboratory investiga-tions. Leucocytosis is common and reflects the transit of activated neu-trophils and monocytes to the site of infection. The most widely used laboratory measure of acute inflammation is C-reactive protein (CRP). Circulating levels of many other acute phase reactants, including fibrinogen, ferritin and complement components, are also increased in response to acute inflammation, while albumin levels are reduced.

units.title: Presenting problems in immune disorders
units.summary: Infections can occur in otherwise healthy individuals, but recurrent infec-tion raises suspicion of an immune deficiency. Depending on the compo-nent of the immune system affected, the infections may involve bacteria, viruses, fungi or protozoa, as summarised in Box 4.5. T-cell deficiencies can involve pathogens from all groups. Infections secondary to immune deficiency occur because of defects in the number or function of phagocytes, B cells, T cells or complement, as described later in this chapter. Intermittent fever has a wide differential diagnosis, including recurrent infection, malignancy and certain rheumatic disorders, such as Still dis-ease, vasculitis and SLE, but systemic autoinflammatory disorders are also a potential cause.

Infections secondary to immune deficiency occur because of defects in the number or function of phagocytes, B cells, T cells or complement, as described later in this chapter.

units.title: Intermittent fever
units.summary: Intermittent fever has a wide differential diagnosis, including recurrent infection, malignancy and certain rheumatic disorders, such as Still dis-ease, vasculitis and SLE, but systemic autoinflammatory disorders are also a potential cause. Systemic autoinflammatory disorders are genetic disorders caused by pathogenic variants in genes responsible for regulating the inflammatory response. The symptoms are caused by activation of intracellular signal-ling pathways involved in the regulation of inflammation, with over-pro-duction of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1. A full clinical history and physical examination should be performed, pay-ing attention to the patient’s ethnic background and any family history of a similar disorder.

units.summary: Loss-of-function pathogenic variants have been identified in almost all the complement pathway proteins (see Fig. While most comple-ment deficiencies are rare, mannose-binding lectin deficiency is com-mon and affects about 5% of the northern European population, many of whom are asymptomatic (see below). units.title: Primary antibody deficiencies
units.summary: Primary antibody deficiencies occur as the result of abnormalities in B-cell function, as summarised in Figure 4.9 and Box 4.9. They are characterised by recurrent bacterial infections, particularly of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tract. The most common caus-ative organisms are encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and H. These disorders usually present in infancy, when the protective benefit of transplacentally derived mater-nal immunoglobulin has waned.

units.title: Primary T-lymphocyte deficiencies

These disorders generally present in childhood, but primary T-cell immunodefi-ciency can also present in adults. Individual conditions are discussed in more detail below.

units.title: Secondary immune deficiencies
units.summary: Secondary immune deficiencies are much more common than primary immune deficiencies and occur when the immune system is compro-mised by external factors (Box 4.12). Common causes include infec-tions, such as HIV and measles, and cytotoxic and immunosuppressive drugs, particularly those used in the management of transplantation, autoimmunity and cancer. Physiological immune deficiency occurs at the extremes of life; the decline of the immune response in the elderly is known as immune senescence (Box 4.13). units.title: Systemic autoinflammatory disorders
units.summary: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is the most common of the sys-temic autoinflammatory disorders, predominantly affecting people of Mediterranean origin. It results from mutations of the MEFV gene, which encodes a protein called pyrin that normally regulates neutrophil-mediated inflammation by indirectly suppressing the production of IL-1. FMF is characterised by recurrent painful attacks of fever, associated with peritonitis, pleuritis and arthritis, which last for a few hours to 4 days, and are associated with markedly increased CRP levels. Symptoms resolve completely between episodes. Mevalonate kinase deficiency, previously known as hyper-IgD syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder that causes recurrent attacks of fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, lymphadenopathy, arthralgia, skin lesions and aphthous ulceration.

units.title: TNF receptor–associated periodic syndrome
units.summary: The TNF receptor–associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS), also known as Hibernian fever, is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by het-erozygote pathogenic variants in the TNFRSF1A gene, which encodes the TNFR1 receptor. The variants cause TNFR1 to be misfolded and internalised causing activation of pro-inflammatory gene expression. The presentation is with recurrent attacks of fever, arthralgia, myalgia, serositis and rashes. During a typical attack, laboratory findings include neutrophilia, increased CRP and elevated IgA levels.

units.title: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS)
units.summary: This disorder includes three phenotypes: familial cold autoinflammatory syn-drome, Muckle–Wells syndrome and neonatal-onset multisystem inflam-matory disease. CAPS results from gain-of-function pathogenic variants of the NLRP3 gene coding cryopyrin, which forms part of the inflammasome. Defects lead to overproduction of IL-1, resulting in the inflammatory manifestations. Treatments are now targeted at the IL-1 pathway, using anakinra or canakinumab.

units.title: Amyloidosis
units.summary: Amyloidosis is the name given to a group of acquired and hereditary dis-orders characterised by the extracellular deposition of insoluble proteins. Amyloidosis is caused by deposits consisting of fibrils of the specific pro-tein involved, linked to glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans and serum amyloid P. Protein accumulation may be localised or systemic, and the clinical manifestations depend on the organ(s) affected. Amyloid diseases are classified by the aetiology and type of protein deposited (Box 4.14).

units.title: Autoimmune disease
units.summary: Autoimmunity can be defined as the presence of immune responses against self-tissue. This may be a harmless phenomenon, identified only by the presence of low-titre autoantibodies or autoreactive T cells. However, if these responses cause significant organ damage, autoim-mune diseases occur. These are a major cause of chronic morbidity and disability, affecting up to 1 in 30 adults at some point during life.

units.title: Allergy
units.summary: The immune system does not normally respond to the many environ-mental substances to which it is exposed on a daily basis. In allergic indi-viduals, however, an initial exposure to a normally harmless exogenous substance (known as an allergen) triggers the production of specific IgE antibodies by activated B cells. These IgE antibodies bind to high-affinity IgE receptors on the surface of mast cells, a step that is not itself associ-ated with clinical sequelae. However, re-exposure to the allergen leads to binding to and cross-links of membrane-bound IgE, which in turn leads to mast cell activation, with release of a variety of vasoactive media-tors (the early phase response; Fig. Common presentations of allergic disease are shown in Box 4.18.

units.summary: Common presentations of allergic disease are shown in Box 4.18. Those that affect the respiratory system and skin are discussed in more detail in Chapter 17 and Chapter 26, respectively. Here we focus on general prin-ciples of the approach to the allergic patient and some specific examples of allergic disease.

units.title: Anaphylaxis
units.summary: The most severe form of IgE-mediated allergy is anaphylaxis, which is a medical emergency. Anaphylaxis is a potentially life-threatening, systemic reaction to an allergen, characterised by circulatory collapse, broncho-spasm, laryngeal stridor, often associated with angioedema, and urti-caria. The risk of death is increased in patients with pre-existing asthma, particularly if this is poorly controlled, and in situations where treatment with adrenaline (epinephrine) is delayed. Further details are provided in the ‘Presenting problems in acute medicine’ section in Chapter 10.

units.summary: Angioedema is characterised by soft-tissue swelling that most frequently affects the face (Fig. 4.13) but can also affect the extremities and gen-italia. Involvement of the larynx or tongue may cause life-threatening respiratory tract obstruction, and oedema of the intestinal mucosa may cause acute abdominal pain.

units.title: Investigations
units.summary: Differentiating the mechanism of angioedema is important in determining the most appropriate treatment. A clinical history of allergy or drug expo-sure can give clues to the underlying diagnosis. If no obvious trigger can be identified, measurement of complement C4 is useful in differentiating hereditary and acquired angioedema from other causes. If C4 levels are low at the time of an acute attack, further investigations should be initi-ated to look for evidence of C1 inhibitor deficiency.

units.title: Management
units.summary: Several approaches can be deployed in the management of allergic indi-viduals, as discussed below. This is indicated in all cases and should be rigorously attempted, with the advice of specialist dietitians and occupational physicians as necessary. Antihistamines are useful in the management of allergy as they inhibit the effects of histamine on tissue H 1 receptors. Long-acting, non-sedating preparations are particularly useful for prophylaxis.

units.title: Hereditary angioedema
units.summary: Hereditary angioedema (HAE), also known as inherited C1 inhibitor defi-ciency, is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by decreased produc-tion or activity of C1 inhibitor protein. This complement regulatory protein inhibits spontaneous activation of the classical complement pathway (see Fig. It also acts as an inhibitor of the kinin cascade, activation of which increases local bradykinin levels, giving rise to local pain and swelling. The angioedema in HAE may be spontaneous or triggered by local trauma or infection.

units.title: Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency
units.summary: This rare disorder is clinically indistinguishable from HAE but presents in late adulthood. It is associated with autoimmune and lymphoproliferative diseases. Most cases are due to the development of autoantibodies to C1 inhibitor, but the condition can also be caused by autoantibodies that activate C1. Treatment of the underlying disorder may induce remission of angioedema.

units.title: Pregnancy and the immune system
units.summary: Major adaptations occur in the immune system during pregnancy so that the mother does not mount an immune response to the developing fetus. These adaptations can influence the risk and severity of certain infectious diseases such as varicella pneumonia (see p. 1307) as well as the activity of some autoimmune diseases. Some considerations for the development and management of immunological diseases during preg-nancy and breastfeeding are summarised in Box 4.20.

units.title: Transplantation and graft rejection
units.summary: Solid organ transplantation inevitably stimulates an aggressive immune response by the recipient, unless the transplant is between monozygotic twins. The type and severity of the rejection response is determined by the genetic disparity between the donor and recipient, the immune sta-tus of the host and the nature of the tissue transplanted (Box 4.21). The most important genetic determinant is the difference between donor and recipient HLA proteins. The extensive polymorphism of these proteins means that donor HLA antigens are almost invariably recognised as for-eign by the recipient immune system, unless an active attempt has been made to minimise incompatibility. Transplant recipients require indefinite treatment with immunosuppres-sive agents.

units.title: Complications of transplant immunosuppression
units.summary: Transplant recipients require indefinite treatment with immunosuppres-sive agents. In general, two or more immunosuppressive drugs are used in synergistic combination in order to minimise adverse effects. These include glucocorticoids, antiproliferative agents such as azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil, and the calcineurin inhibitors ciclosporin and tacrolimus, which inhibit T-cell signalling and prevent lymphocyte activa-tion. Other more targeted immunosuppressives include anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG), which is a cocktail of polyclonal antibodies directed against antigens on the T-cell surface; basiliximab, which is a monoclonal antibody directed against CD25 (IL-2Rα chain), expressed on activated T cells; and belatacept, which selectively inhibits T-cell activation through blockade of CD80/CD86.

units.title: Organ donation
units.summary: The major problem in transplantation is the shortage of organ donors. Cadaveric organ donors are usually previously healthy individuals who experience brainstem death, frequently because of road traffic accidents or cerebrovascular events. Even if organs were obtained from all poten-tial cadaveric donors, their numbers would be insufficient to meet current demands. Altruistic living dona-tion, usually from close relatives, is widely used in renal transplantation.

units.title: Tumour immunology
units.summary: Surveillance by the immune system is critically important in monitoring and removing damaged and mutated cells as they arise. The ability of the immune system to kill cancer cells effectively is influenced by tumour immunogenicity and specificity. Many cancer antigens are poorly expressed and specific antigens can mutate, either spontaneously or in response to treatment, which can result in evasion of immune responses. In addition, the inhibitory pathways that are used to maintain self-tolerance and limit collateral tissue damage during antimicrobial immune responses can be co-opted by cancerous cells to evade immune destruction.

units.title: Nutritional factors in disease
units.summary: The main nutritional components of food are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water. Carbohydrates, proteins, and fats are referred to as macronutrients and are a source of energy. Other nutrients including vitamins, essential amino acids and essential fatty acids must be consumed in the diet to maintain health (Box 5.2). Nutrients come from foods of different types which are consumed intermittently and some-times only occasionally. Obesity is regarded as a global pandemic (syndemic) as it entails disas-trous consequences for human health.

units.title: Disorders of altered energy balance
units.summary: Obesity is regarded as a global pandemic (syndemic) as it entails disas-trous consequences for human health. In 2020, almost 30% of adults in the UK were obese, defined as a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2, compared with 16% in 1995 and 7% in 1980. Moreover, almost 66% of the total UK adult population is overweight (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m 2). The proportion with a normal weight (BMI 18.5–25 kg/m 2) falls to only about 11% by age 65, present-ing a problem for interpreting disease associations, because those 11% at age 65 include very fit people, but also a relatively high proportion who have remained or become thinner through illness. The BMI cut-offs for under-nutrition in adults are shown in Box 5.12.

units.title: Under-nutrition
units.summary: The BMI cut-offs for under-nutrition in adults are shown in Box 5.12. There remain regions of the world, particularly rural Africa and in war zones, where under-nutrition due to famine is endemic, such that up to 20% of adults have BMI < 18.5 kg/m 2 and stunting due to under-nutrition affects 50% of children. Famine is defined as a condition when, in a specific area, a large part of the population is unable to access an adequate amount of food leading to acute severe malnutrition and associated diseases. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that chronic under-nutrition is responsible for more than half of all childhood deaths worldwide.

units.title: Artificial nutrition at the end of life
section_path: Artificial nutrition at the end of life
units.summary: In some situations, assisted nutrition may not reverse weight loss or improve quality and duration of life. Such scenarios may present when approaching the end of life, or with weight loss due to progressive incura-ble disease, such as advanced respiratory or cardiac failure or dementia. A decision not to intervene may then be appropriate. An intervention that merely prolongs life without preserving or adding to its quality is seldom justified as in the patient’s best interest, particularly if the intervention is not without risk itself.

units.title: Nutrition and dementia
units.summary: Weight loss is seen commonly in older people (Box 5.30) or in those with dementia, and nutritional and eating problems are a significant source of concern for those caring for them. • screen for malnutrition including micronutrients and vitamin deficiencies • assess specific eating difficulties (for example the Edinburgh Feeding Evaluation in Dementia questionnaire) • therapeutic trial of oral nutritional supplements.

units.title: Anorexia nervosa
units.summary: Anorexia nervosa (AN) can lead to extreme under-nutrition. Weight loss occurs is similar fashion to starvation with homogeneous loss of body composites (muscle and fat). Anorexia nervosa has the highest mortal-ity both due to complications of malnutrition (including predisposition to life-threatening infections) and suicide. Treatment of anorexia nervosa is aimed at sustained normalised BMI, but micronutrient deficiencies must also be considered, as zinc or iron deficiency can suppress appetite.

units.title: Diseases associated with deficiency and excess of vitamins and minerals
section_path: Diseases associated with deficiency and excess of vitamins and minerals
units.summary: Vitamins are organic compounds with vital roles as co-factors in certain metabolic pathways (Box 5.31). They are categorised into fat-soluble (vitamins A, D, E and K) and water-soluble (vitamins of the B complex group and vitamin C). Recommended daily intakes vary between countries. In the UK, the reference nutrient intake (RNI) has been calculated as the mean plus two standard deviations (SD) of daily intake in the population, which describes intake that satisfies 97.5% of the population. A number of inorganic elements are necessary for structure and growth, as electrolytes, or as co-factors in enzymes and are essential dietary constit-uents for humans (Box 5.37).

units.title: Inorganic micronutrients
section_path: Diseases associated with deficiency and excess of vitamins and minerals
units.summary: A number of inorganic elements are necessary for structure and growth, as electrolytes, or as co-factors in enzymes and are essential dietary constit-uents for humans (Box 5.37). Deficiency is seen when there is inadequate dietary intake or excessive loss from the body. Toxic effects have also been observed from self-medication and disordered absorption or excretion. Examples of clinical toxicity include excess of iron (haemochromatosis or haemosiderosis), fluoride (fluorosis), copper (Wilson disease) and selenium (selenosis, seen in parts of China).

units.title: Multiple Choice Questions
units.summary: In a clinical setting, overweight/ obesity should be assessed using: BMI Waist circumference Observation and clinical judgement Plasma leptin concentration A composite of BMI and full clinical evaluation The recommended approach to assess an individual is to measure BMI (and waist if BMI is < 35 kg/m 2), and to monitor progress using body weight and clinical staging based on evaluation of clinical status using a scheme such as the Edmonton Obesity Staging System. BMI alone provides a useful benchmark, but BMI has relatively poor correlation with body fat content and it does not capture the variable link with symptoms or medical conditions mediated by the disease process of obesity.

units.title: Determinants of health
units.summary: The adverse health and social consequences of poverty are well doc-umented. Typically, with industrialisation, disease patterns change: instead of infections, long-term conditions such as heart disease dom-inate in an older population. Many countries are now experiencing a ‘double burden’. They have large populations still living in poverty that are suffering from problems such as diarrhoea and malnutrition, alongside affluent populations (often in cities) that suffer from chronic illness such as diabetes and heart disease. Climate change is the world’s most important environmental health issue.

units.title: Climate change
units.summary: Climate change is the world’s most important environmental health issue. A combination of increased production of carbon dioxide and habitat destruction, both caused primarily by human activity, is the main cause. The temperature of the globe is rising, the climate is being affected, and if the trend is not reversed, sea levels will rise and rainfall patterns will be altered so that severe weather events, droughts and floods will become more common. These have already claimed millions of lives during the past 20 years and have adversely affected the lives of many more.

units.title: The life course
units.summary: The determinants of health operate over the whole lifespan. Exposure to adverse socioeconomic and built environments, along with values and behaviours acquired during childhood and adolescence, can have a profound influence on educational outcomes, job prospects and risk of disease. These can have a strong influence, for example, on whether a young person takes up a damaging behaviour like smoking, develops severe mental health problems or is the victim of violence or trauma. Influences on health can even operate before birth.

units.title: Health improvement
units.summary: The complexity of the interactions between physical, social and economic determinants of health means that preventing ill health and promoting wellbeing is often difficult. Moreover, the life course perspective illustrates that it may be necessary to intervene early in life or even before birth, to prevent important disease in later life. Successful prevention is likely to require many interventions across the life course and at several levels in the hierarchy of systems. The examples below illustrate this principle.

units.title: Alcohol
units.summary: Alcohol use is an increasingly important risk factor underlying global bur-den of disease (see Fig. Reasons for increasing rates of alcohol-related harm vary by place and time but include the falling price of alcohol (in real terms), increased availability and cultural change fostering higher levels of consumption. Public, professional and governmental concern has now led to a range of policy interventions, including a minimum price being charged for a unit of alcohol, tightening of licensing regulations and curtailment of promotional activity in some countries. However, even more aggressive public health and policy measures will be needed to reverse the levels of harm in the population.

units.title: Smoking
units.summary: Smoking is one of the top three risk factors underlying global burden of disease (see Fig. It is responsible for the substantial majority of cases of lung cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and most smokers die either from these respiratory diseases or from cardiovascular disease. Smoking also causes cancers of other organs, and increases the risk of peripheral vascular disease, stroke and peptic ulceration. Maternal smoking is an important cause of fetal growth restriction.

units.title: Obesity
units.summary: Obesity is an increasingly important risk factor underlying global burden of disease (see Fig. The weight distribution of almost the whole population is shifting upwards – the slim are becoming less slim while the overweight and obese are becoming more so. In the UK, this translates into a 1-kilogram increase in weight per adult per year (on average over the adult popula-tion). The current obesity epidemic cannot be explained simply by individ-ual behaviour and poor choice but also requires an understanding of the obesogenic environment that encourages people to eat more and exercise less.

units.title: Principles of screening and immunisation
units.summary: Screening is the application of a screening test to a large number of asymptomatic people with the aim of reducing morbidity or mortality from a disease. WHO have identified a set of (Wilson and Jungner) criteria to guide health systems in deciding when it is appropriate to implement screening programmes. • Is the disease an important public health problem? • Is there a suitable screening test available? Immunisation can confer immunity to specific infectious diseases and be either passive (through injected antibodies, such as the monoclo-nal palivizumab against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection given to premature infants) or active (through administration of a vaccine).

WHO have identified a set of (Wilson and Jungner) criteria to guide health systems in deciding when it is appropriate to implement screening programmes. • Is the disease an important public health problem? • Is there a suitable screening test available?

units.title: Immunisation
units.summary: Immunisation can confer immunity to specific infectious diseases and be either passive (through injected antibodies, such as the monoclo-nal palivizumab against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection given to premature infants) or active (through administration of a vaccine). Immunisation invokes antibody and/or cell-mediated immunity and can lead to both short- and longer-term protection in the person who is vac-cinated. Immunisation has also been used to eradicate a disease, such as occurred in the smallpox eradication programme and is currently being targeted in the polio eradication programme. As well as direct effects of vaccination, a number of indirect effects can occur, such as protection of individuals who are vaccinated through altering disease transmission leading to ‘herd immunity’; or reduction of antibiotic resist-ance through selective reduction of pneumococcal serogroups that are associated with antibiotic resistance.

units.title: Epidemiology
units.summary: Epidemiological research complements that based on animal, cell and tissue models, the findings of which do not always translate to humans. For example, only a minority of drug discoveries from laboratory research are found to be effective when tested in people. However, differentiating causes from mere non-causal associations is a considerable challenge for epidemiology. This is because while labora-tory researchers can directly manipulate conditions to isolate and under-stand causes, such approaches are impossible in free-living populations.

units.title: Health informatics and health information systems
section_path: Health informatics and health information systems
units.summary: An epidemic, as defined by the World Health Organization, occurs when ‘in a community or region [the] cases of an illness, specific health-related behaviour, or other health-related events [are] clearly in excess of normal expectancy’. Epidemics that are small-scale or confined to a small geo-graphic area are informally referred to as ‘outbreaks’. Epidemics are regularly caused where preventative measures break down; examples include breaches of food safety procedures in restau-rants resulting in outbreaks of enteropathogenic E. coli infection, failure to adequately maintain cooling towers causing Legionella infections and falls in vaccination coverage resulting in measles epidemics.

units.title: Principles of infection
units.summary: The concept of an infectious agent was established by Robert Koch in the 19th century (Box 7.1). Although fulfilment of ‘Koch’s postulates’ became the standard for confirming the cause of an infection, many infectious agents do not fulfil Koch’s postulates (e.g. uncultivable organ-isms and the causes of endogenous infections), and the postulates are now of mainly historical interest. The groups of infectious agents that are now recognised are described in the following sections. The human body is colonised by large numbers of microorganisms (col-lectively termed the human microbiota).

units.title: Host–pathogen interactions
units.summary: A ‘pathogen’ is a microorganism that can cause infection. The manifes-tations of infection, including a pathogen’s ability to cause severe disease in a previously healthy host, are affected by its ‘virulence’. Virulence is determined by the number and type of disease-causing proteins and other factors that it can produce (‘virulence factors’). • Primary pathogens cause disease in a proportion of individuals to whom they are exposed, regardless of the host’s immunological status.

units.title: Indirect detection of pathogens
units.summary: Tests may be used to detect the host’s immune (e.g. antibody or T-cell) response to a specific microorganism, enabling the diagnosis of infection with organisms that are difficult to detect by other methods or are no longer present in the host. The term ‘serology’ describes tests carried out on serum and includes both antigen (direct) and antibody (indirect) detection. Detection of antigen is described above in the section on detection of components of organisms.

units.title: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing
units.summary: If growth of microorganisms in culture is inhibited by the addition of an antimicrobial agent, the organism is considered to be susceptible to that antimicrobial. The lowest concentration of the antimicrobial agent at which growth is inhibited is the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), and the lowest concentration that causes cell death is the mini-mum bactericidal concentration (MBC). If the MIC is less than or equal to a predetermined breakpoint threshold, the organism is considered susceptible, and if the MIC is greater than the breakpoint, it is resistant. Breakpoints are determined for antimicrobial agents using a combination of pharmacokinetic and clinical data.

units.title: Outbreaks of infection
units.summary: Descriptive terms for infectious disease outbreaks are defined in Box 7.10. Confirmation of an infectious disease outbreak usually requires evidence from ‘typing’ that the causal organisms have identical phenotypic and/or genotypic characteristics. When an outbreak of infection is suspected, a case definition is agreed. The number of cases that meet the case definition is then assessed by case-finding, using methods ranging from administration of questionnaires to national reporting systems.

units.title: Immunisation
units.summary: Passive immunisation is achieved by administering antibodies targeting a specific pathogen. Antibodies are obtained from blood, so confer some of the infection risks associated with blood products. The protection afforded by passive immunisation is immediate but of short duration (a few weeks or months); it is used to prevent or attenuate infection before or after exposure (Box 7.13). Active immunisation is achieved by vaccination with whole organisms, organism components or nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) (Box 7.14).

units.title: Antimicrobial stewardship
units.summary: Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) refers to the systems and processes applied to a population to optimise the use of antimicrobial agents. The populations referred to here may be a nation, region, hospital, or a unit within a health-care organisation (e.g. AMS aims to improve patient outcomes and reduce antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Elements of AMS include treatment guidelines, antimicrobial formularies and ward rounds by infection specialists.

units.title: Antimycobacterial agents
units.summary: Isoniazid is bactericidal for replicating bacteria and bacteriostatic for non-replicating bacteria. It is activated by mycobacterial catalase-per-oxidase (KatG) and inhibits the InhA gene product, a reductase involved in mycolic acid synthesis. Mutations in KatG or InhA result in isoniazid resistance, which was reported in 15% of cases of M. Isoniazid is well absorbed orally and metabolised by acetylation in the liver.

units.title: Antifungal agents
units.summary: The azoles (imidazoles and triazoles) inhibit synthesis of ergosterol, a constituent of the fungal cell membrane. Side-effects vary but include gastrointestinal upset, hepatitis and rash. Azoles are inhibitors of cytochrome P450 enzymes, so they tend to increase exposure to cytochrome P450-metabolised drugs. Miconazole, econazole, clotrimazole and ketoconazole are relatively toxic and therefore administered topically.

units.title: 2. Resisting cell death
units.summary: There are three principal mechanisms through which cell death occurs in healthy tissues: apoptosis, autophagy and necrosis. It is frequently found at markedly reduced rates in cancers, particularly those of high grade or those resistant to treatment. The cellular apoptotic system has regulatory elements that sense intrinsic and extrinsic pro-apoptotic signals. This initiates a cas-cade of proteolysis and cell disassembly with nuclear fragmentation, chromosomal condensation and shrinking of the cell with loss of inter-cellular contact, followed by cellular fragmentation and the formation of apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed by neighbouring cells.

units.summary: The ‘cell cycle’ is tightly controlled at different stages. Normal cells grow and divide in response to external signals, typically growth factors. These are able to bind to cell surface–bound receptors that activate an intra-cellular tyrosine kinase–mediated signalling cascade, ultimately leading to changes in gene expression that promote cellular proliferation and growth. units.title: 4. Evading growth suppressors
units.summary: The cell cycle is orchestrated by a number of molecular mechanisms, most importantly by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs). Cyclins bind to CDKs and are regulated by both activating and inacti-vating phosphorylation, with two main checkpoints at G 1 /S and G 2 /M transition. The genes that inhibit progression play an important part in tumour prevention and are referred to as tumour suppressor genes (e.g. The products of these genes deactivate the cyclin–CDK complexes and are thus able to halt the cell cycle.

units.title: 5. Enabling replicative immortality
units.summary: Normal cells have a limited number of divisions before they are una-ble to divide further (senescence) or before they die (crisis). These limits are controlled by telomeric DNA sequences, which protect and stabilise chromosomal ends. During replication, telomeres shorten progressively as small fragments of telomeric DNA are lost with successive cycles of replication. This shortening process represents a mitotic clock and even-tually prevents the cell from dividing further.

units.title: 6. Inducing angiogenesis
units.summary: All cells and body tissues require sustenance in the form of nutrients and oxygen, as well as an ability to evacuate metabolic waste products and carbon dioxide. Tumours require a functional vascular network to ensure continued growth and are unable to grow beyond 1 mm 3 without stimulating the development of a vascular supply through angiogenesis (Figs. Angiogenesis is dependent on the production of angiogenic growth factors, of which vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and plate-let-derived growth factor (PDGF) are the best characterised. During tumour progression, an angiogenic switch is activated and remains on, causing normally quiescent vasculature to develop new vessels continu-ally to help sustain expanding tumour growth.

units.title: 7. Activating invasion and metastasis
units.summary: The ability to invade neighbouring tissue determines whether a tumour is benign or malignant. Clinically, the presence of metastases often determines whether a cancer can be cured. The invasion-metastatic cascade is a complex multistep process. The initiation of this process is enabled by epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT).

units.title: 8. Deregulating cellular energetics
units.summary: Under aerobic conditions, oxidative phosphorylation functions as the main metabolic pathway for energy production; cells process glucose, first to pyruvate via glycolysis and thereafter to carbon dioxide in the mitochondria. While under anaerobic conditions, glycolysis is favoured to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Cancer cells can reprogram their glucose metabolism to limit energy production to glycolysis, even in the presence of oxygen. Up-regulation of glucose transporters, such as GLUT1, is the main mechanism through which aerobic glycolysis is achieved.

units.title: 9. Tumour-promoting inflammation
units.summary: Almost all tumours show infiltration with immune cells on pathological investigation and historically this finding was thought to represent an attempt by the immune system to eradicate the cancer. It is now clear that tumour-associated inflammatory responses contribute to several hallmark capabilities and promote tumour formation and cancer progres-sion. Immune cells may promote invasive behaviour, and bioactive mole-cules such as cytokines, growth factors and pro-angiogenic factors may be released into the tumour microenvironment. In particular, the release of reactive oxygen species, which are actively mutagenic, will accelerate the genetic evolution of surrounding cancer cells, enhancing growth and contributing to cancer progression.

units.title: 10. Evading immune destruction
units.summary: Cancer cells continuously shed antigens into the circulatory system, prompting an immune response that includes cytotoxic T-cell, natural killer cell and macrophage production. The immune system is thought to provide continuous surveillance, with resultant elimination of cells that undergo malignant transformation. However, if not all cancer cells are eliminated there may be a period of equilibrium where tumour growth is controlled by the immune system and cancer cells may enter a dormant state, sometimes for many years. Alternatively, cancer cells may escape immune control and grow into clinically apparent tumours.

units.title: Environmental and genetic determinants of cancer
section_path: Environmental and genetic determinants of cancer
units.summary: The majority of cancers do not have a single cause, but rather are the result of a complex interaction between genetic factors and exposure to environmental carcinogens. These are often tumour type-specific, but some general principles do apply. Environmental triggers for cancer have mainly been identified through epidemiological studies that examine patterns of distribution of cancers in patients in whom parameters such as age, sex, presence of other illnesses, social class, geography and diet differ. Sometimes these give strong pointers to the molecular or cellular causes of the disease, such as the association between aflatoxin production within contaminated food supplies and hepatocellular carcinomas.

units.title: Multidisciplinary teams
units.summary: The multidisciplinary team (MDT) is well established in oncology and meets on a regular basis to provide a forum for patient-centred, inter-disciplinary communication to coordinate care and decision-making. It is a platform on which individual clinicians can discuss complex cases or situations and draw on the collective experience of the team member-ship to decide on the best approach for an individual patient. This can be particularly important when discussing patients with a rare or complex condition or in an unusual situation. As a minimum, most MDTs include a radiologist, pathologist, specialist physician, specialist surgeon, radiation oncologist, medical oncologist, nurse specialist, auditor and scheduler.

These are sometimes called ‘red flag’ symptoms of cancer (Box 8.9). Patients may present with consti-tutional symptoms such as unexplained weight loss, fatigue or fevers. Oncological emergencies are a group of potentially life-threatening con-ditions that occur as a direct result of cancer or its treatment.

units.summary: Surgery has a pivotal role in the management of cancer. It is the main curative management of most solid cancers. In early localised cases of colorectal, breast and lung cancer, cure rates are high with surgery. Radiotherapy (radiation therapy) involves treating cancers with ionising radiation such as X-rays, gamma rays, electrons or charged atoms.

units.title: Radiotherapy
units.summary: Radiotherapy (radiation therapy) involves treating cancers with ionising radiation such as X-rays, gamma rays, electrons or charged atoms. Ionising radiation kills cancer cells by two mechanisms: directly damag-ing cancer DNA or indirectly by triggering the formation of very reactive molecules (free radicals) that also damage cancer DNA. Radiotherapy can be given alongside systemic therapy and some anti-cancer thera-pies act as radiosensitisers, which can make cancer cells more sensitive to radiation and allow reduced radiation doses. There are several types of radiation therapy including external beam radiotherapy, stereotactic radiotherapy (a precisely targeted form of high-dose external beam radiotherapy), proton beam therapy, brachytherapy (internal or locally applied radiotherapy) and radioisotope therapy (sys-temically delivered radiotherapy).

units.title: Systemic anti-cancer therapy
units.summary: Systemic anti-cancer therapy (SACT) is a collective term to describe the growing number of differing drug therapies used to treat cancer. These drugs reach throughout the body to treat cancer cells wherever they may be. Increasingly, treatment is tailored to a patient’s particular cancer and its molecular profile, allowing more personalised therapy. Whilst most anti-cancer therapies cause some side-effects, most of these can be managed with supportive medicines at home.

units.title: Evaluation of treatment
units.summary: In advanced or metastatic cancer, the evaluation of treatment is an ongoing process and includes assessments of treatment response, toxicity and quality of life. Clinical evaluation, patient-reported outcome measures, biochemical monitoring (including sequential tumour marker analysis), and radiological evaluation are commonly used to determine whether a treatment is being effective. Uniform criteria have been estab-lished to measure these, primarily measuring morphologic criteria using the response evaluation criteria in solid tumours (RECIST; Box 8.20), or iRECIST for immunotherapy treatments. Measurement of metabolic criteria using positron emission tomography (PET) response criteria in solid tumours (PERCIST) can be used to assess metabolic response depending on sequential 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET activity in tumours on treatment.

units.title: Late toxicity of therapy
units.summary: The late toxicities of treatment for cancer are particularly important for patients where multimodality therapy is given with curative intent, where the patient is young and as more patients are living longer. This can cause considerable morbidity: for example, radiotherapy can retard bone and cartilage growth, impair intellect and cognitive function, and cause dysfunction of the hypothalamus, pituitary and thyroid glands. Late con-sequences of cytotoxic chemotherapy include heart failure due to cardi-otoxicity, pulmonary fibrosis, nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity. Premature gonadal failure can result from cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiotherapy and leave a patient subfertile.

units.title: Cancer clinical trials
units.summary: Cancer clinical trials are embedded within routine practice in oncol-ogy. Close collaboration with laboratory scientists, active recruitment of cancer patients into clinical trials and robust translational research have led to many new cancer treatments, personalised therapies and a transformation of cancer management over the last 20 years. As many anti-cancer drugs are expected to have toxicities, which may ultimately limit the deliverable dose, clinical trials in cancer differ from trials of other medicines. • Phase I cancer clinical trials take treatments of interest from labo-ratory studies and test them in patients with advanced cancer for whom no other standard anti-cancer treatment exists.

Invasive ductal carcinoma with or without ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common histology, accounting for 70%, whilst invasive lobular carcinoma accounts for most of the remain-ing cases. DCIS constitutes 20% of breast cancers detected by mam-mography screening. It is multifocal in one-third of women and has a high risk of becoming invasive (10% at 5 years following excision only). units.title: Ovarian cancer
units.summary: Most ovarian cancers are epithelial in origin (90%), and up to 7% of women with ovarian cancer have a positive family history. Patients often present late in ovarian cancer with vague abdominal discomfort, low back pain, bloating, altered bowel habit and weight loss. Occasionally, peritoneal deposits are palpable as an omental ‘cake’ and nodules in the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph nodules). Genetic and environmental factors play a role.

units.title: Endometrial cancer
units.summary: Endometrial cancer primarily affects post-menopausal women, with a peak incidence at 65–75 years of age. Mortality from endometrial cancer is currently falling; however, 25% of patients will not survive for 5 years or more. The most common presentation is with post-menopausal bleed-ing, which often results in early detection of the disease before distant spread has occurred. Oestrogen plays an important role in the pathogenesis of endometrial cancer, and factors that increase the duration of oestrogen exposure, such as nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause and unopposed HRT, increase the risk.

units.title: Cervical cancer
units.summary: Cervical cancer is the leading cause of death from gynaecological can-cer worldwide. The incidence is decreasing in high-income countries as a result of HPV vaccination and screening programmes, but continues to rise in low- and middle-income nations. Early-stage cervical cancer may not cause symptoms. In the UK the most common presentation of these cancers is with an abnormal smear test through the cervical cancer screening programme.

units.title: Head and neck tumours
units.summary: Head and neck cancers are typically squamous tumours that arise in the nasopharynx, hypopharynx and larynx. They are most common in older adult males, but oropharyngeal cancers now occur with increasing frequency in a younger cohort of patients, including in women. The rising incidence of oropharyngeal cancers, especially in high-income countries, is thought to be secondary to HPV infection. Presentation depends on the location of the primary tumour and the extent of disease.

units.title: Neuropathic versus nociceptive pain
units.summary: Neuropathic pain is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system. Pain arises from damage to the peripheral nerves (see Box 27.96) or central nervous system (CNS), when it is termed central pain. Neuropathic pain may be acute, such as in sciatica, but is most debilitating when it becomes chronic, impacting on quality of life and function. The clinical features of neuropathic pain are detailed in Box 9.1.

Pharmacological mod-ulation of these neurotransmitters and their target receptors underlie the mode of action of many analgesic medications. Pain signals from the spinal cord travel to the sensory cortex via the thalamus.

units.title: Chronic and neuropathic pain mechanisms
units.summary: The peripheral and central nervous systems adapt to the presence of pain, especially in response to sustained tissue damage, a process called neuronal plasticity. In chronic pain this produces prolonged changes in the pathways involved in detecting and processing nocicep tive stimuli. units.title: Pain scoring systems
units.summary: A wide range of tools have been developed to assess pain (Box 9.2). Unidimensional tools are used to grade the severity of pain and can be carried out verbally using the Numerical Rating Scale, which grades pain from 0 to 10, or by asking a patient to indicate their score on a Visual Analogue Scale from 0 to 10. Multidimensional tools include the severity, distribution, character and psychological/functional impacts of pain. Verbal self-reporting of pain is seen as the gold standard, but not all patients will manage this.

units.title: Acute pain management
units.summary: The underlying condition causing the pain should be treated whenever possible. Pain relief can be provided through immobilisation of the painful area using slings, braces and splints or by positioning the patient appro-priately. Painful wounds can be dressed and the application of heat or cold can provide relief. Early physiotherapy input can help maintain func-tion and promote functional recovery. The choice of initial medication is based on clinical assessment and the severity of the pain.

units.title: Pharmacological management
units.summary: The choice of initial medication is based on clinical assessment and the severity of the pain. A simple numerical rating scale can be used to assess severity, dividing pain into mild (score 1–3), moderate (score 4–6) and severe (score 7–10). Mild pain can usually be managed using non-opioids, while moderate and severe pain may require the short-term use of opioid medications. A multimodal approach is recommended for acute pain; combining paracetamol with a non-steroidal anti-inflamma-tory drug (NSAID) or opioid can produce increased benefit while reducing individual drug dosage requirement.

units.title: Pain management – non-cancer-related chronic pain
units.summary: When a definitive underlying disease has not been identified, the manage-ment of chronic pain focuses on supporting the patient with the psycho-logical, emotional and functional impacts to improve quality of life. In 2021 the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) published guidance on managing primary chronic pain, which recommends multidisci-plinary non-pharmacological interventions as the mainstay of treatment. The only pharmacological agents recommended are antidepressants (amitrip-tyline, duloxetine, citalopram, sertraline or paroxetine), which may improve pain and sleep. The guidelines advise against initiating any other drug ther-apy, including paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, gabapentin and pregabalin. The principles of managing chronic primary pain largely apply to second-ary chronic pain.

units.title: Pain management – cancer-related pain
units.summary: Acute cancer pain is generally somatic or visceral nociceptive pain and occurs in the context of investigations or surgical intervention. The assessment and management is broadly similar to acute pain arising from other causes. Concern over impending diagnostic biopsy and scan results can increase the distress related to acute pain. It is estimated that about two-thirds of patients with cancer experi-ence moderate or severe chronic pain, and a quarter have three or more different sites of pain. Chronic cancer pain is most commonly of mixed aetiology with a combination of nociceptive and neuropathic elements.
