units.title: Miscellaneous conditions
units.summary: This is characterised by severe pain in the front of the lower leg, aggra-vated by exercise and relieved by rest. Symptoms result from fascial compression of the muscles in the anterior tibial compartment and may be associated with foot drop. This is a common nerve entrapment syndrome caused by compression of the median nerve at the wrist. It presents with numbness, tingling and pain in a median nerve distribution.

units.title: Pigmented villonodular synovitis
units.summary: Pigmented villonodular synovitis is an uncommon proliferative disorder of synovium, which typically affects young adults. It is caused by a somatic chromosomal translocation in synovial cells that places the CSF1 gene downstream of the COL6A3 gene promoter. The result is local over-production of M-CSF, which causes accumulation of macrophages in the joint. The presentation is with joint swelling, limitation of movement and local discomfort.

units.title: Functional anatomy and physiology
units.summary: The skin covers just under 2 m 2 in the average adult. The outer layer is the epidermis, a stratified squamous epithelium consisting mainly of kerati-nocytes. The epidermis is attached to, but separated from, the underly-ing dermis by the basement membrane. The dermis is less cellular and supports blood vessels, nerves and epidermal-derived appendages (hair follicles and sweat glands).

units.title: Investigation of skin disease
units.summary: A hand-held or freestanding magnifying lens used under good lighting conditions (ideally daylight) is valuable for examination of the skin. Wood’s light is a long-wavelength UVA/short-wavelength visible (violet) light source that can be used in various ways. In hypopigmentation, such as in vitiligo, it can help in appreciating the extent of disease. In pig-mented conditions, such as melasma, it can determine whether pigmen-tation is mainly epidermal (sharp cut-off under Wood’s lamp) or mixed epidermal and dermal (ill-defined cut-off).

units.title: Blisters
units.summary: A blister is a fluid-filled collection in the skin. The term vesicle is used for small lesions and bulla for larger lesions. Blistering occurs due to loss of cell adhesion within the epidermis or subepidermal region (see Fig. The clinical presentation depends on the site or level of blistering within the skin, which in turn reflects the underlying cause.

units.title: Itch (pruritus)
units.summary: Itch describes the unpleasant sensation that leads to scratching or rub-bing. The terms ‘itch’ and ‘pruritus’ are synonymous; however, ‘pruritus’ is often used when itch is generalised. Itch can arise from primary cuta-neous disease or be secondary to systemic disease, which may cause itch by central or peripheral mechanisms. Even when the mechanism is peripheral, there are not always signs of primary skin disease.

units.title: Leg ulcers
units.summary: Leg ulcer is not a diagnosis, but a symptom of an underlying disease in which there is complete epidermal loss, leaving dermal layers exposed. Ulcers on the lower leg are frequently caused by vascular disease but there are other causes, as summarised in Box 26.10. A detailed history of the onset and course of leg ulceration and predis-posing conditions should be elicited. The site and surrounding skin should be assessed.

units.title: Abnormal pigmentation
units.summary: Loss of skin pigmentation (depigmentation), reduction in pigmentation (hypopigmentation) and increased pigment (hyperpigmentation) are features of a variety of disorders. A detailed history and examination, including use of a Wood’s light, are required to establish the diagnosis. Investigations will depend on the presentation. For example, microscopy of skin scrapings should be undertaken if hypopigmentation is associated with inflammation and scaling; screening for autoimmune disease may be required if vitiligo is suspected; and investigation for endocrine dis-ease or the porphyrias may be appropriate in hyperpigmentation.

units.title: Acute skin failure: erythroderma and epidermal necrolysis
section_path: Acute skin failure: erythroderma and epidermal necrolysis
units.summary: Acute skin failure is a medical emergency, and this broad term includes erythroderma and epidermal necrolysis presentations. Several conditions can cause widespread and acute failure of many skin functions (see Box 26.1), including thermoregulation, fluid balance control and barrier to infection. Many of these conditions involve widespread dilatation of the dermal vasculature and can provoke high-output cardiac failure; they are also associated with increased protein loss from the skin and often from the gut. Many lead to acute skin failure by causing erythroderma (ery-thema affecting at least 90% of the body surface area), although severe autoimmune blistering diseases and the spectrum of Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) disease can produce acute skin failure without erythroderma.

units.title: Principles of management of skin disease
section_path: Principles of management of skin disease
units.summary: General measures that apply in all skin diseases include establishment of the correct diagnosis, removal of precipitating or aggravating factors, use of safe, effective treatments and consideration of the patient holistically, considering the impact of the disease on quality of life and the person’s support network. The psychological impact of chronic skin diseases should not be under-estimated, and it is important to remember that psychiatric illness can also manifest as skin disease, such as in delusions of infestation or trichotillomania. Careful clinical assessment is essential, and any management strategy must also include approaches to address the psychological well-being of the patient. Topical treatments are first-line therapy for most skin diseases, many of which can be treated effectively by topical agents alone. Selection of the appropriate active drug/ingredient and vehicle is essential.

units.title: Topical treatments
section_path: Principles of management of skin disease
units.summary: Topical treatments are first-line therapy for most skin diseases, many of which can be treated effectively by topical agents alone. Selection of the appropriate active drug/ingredient and vehicle is essential. Ointments are preferred to creams for dry skin conditions, such as chronic eczemas, as they are more hydrating and contain fewer preservatives than creams, and so allergy risk is reduced. However, patients find creams easier to apply and thus compliance may be better.

units.title: Phototherapy and photochemotherapy
section_path: Principles of management of skin disease
units.summary: Ultraviolet radiation (UVR) treatments (most commonly, narrowband ultra-violet B and psoralen–ultraviolet A (PUVA)) are used in the management of many different diseases and are invaluable therapies to have available. The best evidence for their efficacy is in psoriasis, atopic eczema, vitiligo and chronic urticaria, although there is also evidence that UVB is helpful in treating generalised itch associated with chronic kidney disease (urae-mic pruritus) and a range of other diverse skin conditions. Psoralens are natural photosensitisers found in many plants. They intercalate between the strands of DNA and, on excitation with UVA, cross-link the DNA strands.

units.title: Systemic therapies
section_path: Principles of management of skin disease
units.summary: General information is provided here for drugs used in a range of skin diseases; details of other drugs are provided in disease-specific sections. Antibiotics are widely used for their anti-infective properties, particularly for staphylococcal and streptococcal skin infections. In these indications, the correct antibiotic should be selected, based on bacterial sensitivity and patient factors. As examples, oral flucloxacillin may be indicated for clinically infected eczema, intravenous flucloxacillin for cellulitis, and clar-ithromycin for a patient with a staphylococcal carbuncle who is penicillin allergic.

units.title: Dermatological surgery
section_path: Principles of management of skin disease
units.summary: Most dermatological surgical procedures are performed under local anaesthetic. Knowledge of local anatomy is essential, particularly the locations of vessels and nerves. In certain sites, such as the fingers, soles of the feet and the nose, local cutaneous nerve blocks are useful. Some sites are associated with particular risks, such as keloidal scarring on the upper trunk of young patients, unsightly scars over the scapulae, and poor healing and risk of ulceration following procedures on the lower legs.

units.title: Non-surgical treatments
section_path: Principles of management of skin disease
units.summary: Cryotherapy is a destructive treatment using liquid nitrogen to cause cell-wall and membrane destruction and cell death. Liquid nitrogen can be applied either with a cotton bud or, more effectively, with a spray gun. A wide variety of conditions can be treated but it is essential for the correct diagnosis to be made first, if necessary, by diagnostic biopsy. Cryotherapy should not be used to treat mel-anocytic naevi.

units.title: Skin tumours
units.summary: The incidence of NMSC has increased dramatically in recent decades and basal cell carcinoma (BCC) accounts for more than 70% of cases. In Europe, the ratio of BCC to SCC is 4–5:1 in immunocompetent patients. It is a malignant tumour that rarely metastasises; it is thought to derive from immature pluripotent epidermal cells and is composed of cells with similarities to basal layer epidermis and appendages. Lesions typically occur at sites of moderate sun exposure, particularly the face, and grow slowly. In practice, it is often difficult to distinguish between skin cancer and a benign lesion on clinical grounds; if there is any doubt, biopsy and histol-ogy are required.

units.title: Benign skin lesions
units.summary: In practice, it is often difficult to distinguish between skin cancer and a benign lesion on clinical grounds; if there is any doubt, biopsy and histol-ogy are required. Notably, benign melanocytic naevi and basal cell papil-loma (seborrhoeic keratosis) can often be mistaken for melanoma, even by dermatologists. Keratoacanthoma, while benign, is also commonly considered to be an invasive SCC on clinical grounds. This benign tumour has a striking clinical presentation of rapid growth over weeks to months and subsequent spontaneous resolution.

There are two main presentations: bullous impetigo, caused by a staphylococcal epidermolytic toxin, and non-bullous impetigo (Fig. 26.20), which can be caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or strep-tococci, or both together. are the most common agents in temperate climates, whereas streptococcal impetigo is more often seen in hot, humid areas.

units.title: Fungal infections
units.summary: Fungal skin infections can be superficial (dermatophytes and yeasts) or, less commonly, deep (chromomycosis or sporotrichosis); the latter are seen more often in tropical climates or in the immunocompromised. Dermatophyte infections (ringworm) are extremely common and usually caused by fungi of the Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton species. The fungi can originate from soil (geophilic), animals (zoophilic) or be confined to human skin (anthropophilic). units.title: Infestations
units.summary: Scabies is a common condition, caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei. It spreads in households and environments where there is intimate per-sonal contact. The diagnosis is made by identifying the scabietic burrow (definition: a linear or curvilinear papule, caused by a burrowing scabies mite – Fig. 26.28) and visualising the mite (by extracting with a needle or using a dermatoscope).

units.title: Acne and rosacea
units.summary: Acne is chronic inflammation of the pilosebaceous units. It is extremely common, generally starts during puberty and has been estimated to affect over 90% of adolescents. It is usually most severe in later adoles-cence but can persist into the thirties and forties, particularly in females (Box 26.16). units.title: Eczemas
units.summary: The term ‘eczema’ derives from the Greek word ‘to boil’ and is synony-mous with the other descriptive term, ‘dermatitis’. Eczema (dermatitis) describes a clinical and histological pattern, which can be acute or chronic and has several causes. Acutely, epidermal oedema (spongiosis) and intra-epidermal vesiculation (producing multilocular blisters) predominate, whereas with chronicity there is more epidermal thickening (acanthosis). Vasodilatation and T-cell lymphocytic infiltration of the upper dermis also occur.

units.title: Psoriasis and other erythematous scaly eruptions
section_path: Psoriasis and other erythematous scaly eruptions
units.summary: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory, hyperproliferative skin disease. It is characterised by well-defined, erythematous scaly plaques, particularly affecting extensor surfaces, scalp and nails, and usually follows a relaps-ing and remitting course. Psoriasis affects approximately 1.5%–3% of populations of European ancestry but is less common in Asian, South American and African populations. It occurs equally in both sexes and at any age; although it is uncommon under the age of 5 years, more than 50% of patients present before the age of 30 years.

units.title: Lichenoid eruptions
units.summary: It typically presents as a pruritic rash; the mucosae, hair and nails may also be involved. The disease probably has an autoimmune basis since there is an asso-ciation with inflammatory bowel disease, primary biliary cholangitis, autoimmune hepatitis, hepatitis B and C, alopecia areata, myasthenia gravis and thymoma. There are also similarities with graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Lichen planus can occasionally occur in families and possible HLA associations have been reported but there is no clear inheritance pattern.

units.title: Urticaria
units.summary: Urticaria (‘hives’) is caused by localised dermal oedema secondary to a temporary increase in capillary permeability. If oedema involves subcuta-neous or submucosal layers, the term angioedema is used. Acute urticaria may be associated with angioedema of the lips, face, tongue, throat and, rarely, wheezing, abdominal pain, headaches and even anaphylaxis. Urticaria present for less than six weeks is defined as acute, and chronic if it continues for more than six weeks.

units.title: Bullous diseases
units.summary: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is a medical emergency, as the exten-sive mucocutaneous blistering is associated with a high mortality rate. It is usually drug-induced (see Box 26.35), with anticonvulsants, sulphona-mides, sulphonylureas, NSAIDs, allopurinol and antiretroviral therapy often implicated. Usually 1–4 weeks after drug commencement, the patient becomes systemically unwell and often pyrexial. Erythema and blistering develop, initially on the trunk but rapidly involving all skin; an early warn-ing sign is cutaneous pain. There are various subtypes of immunobullous disease that affect patients of different ages and have clinical characteristics (Box 26.27).

units.title: Immunobullous diseases
units.summary: There are various subtypes of immunobullous disease that affect patients of different ages and have clinical characteristics (Box 26.27). The key investigation is an elliptical biopsy taken from the edge of a recent blister (Box 26.28). The sample is halved: one half is put in formalin for subse-quent histology, while the other is sent fresh for direct immunofluores-cence. Serum should also be sent for indirect immunofluorescence in suspected immunobullous disease.

units.title: Pigmentation disorders
units.summary: Disorders causing hypopigmentation and/or depigmentation include: • pityriasis alba: depigmented areas on the face, particularly in children, with or without scale and usually considered to be eczematous • pityriasis versicolor: hypopigmentation or, less commonly, hyperpig-mentation can occur • idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis: multiple small areas of depigmen-tation arising in chronically sun-exposed skin • Diffuse hyperpigmentation: most commonly due to hypermel-anosis but other pigments may be deposited in the skin, such as orange discoloration with carotenaemia and bronze with haemochromatosis. • Endocrine pigmentation: may occur in several conditions. Melasma (chloasma) describes discrete patches of facial pigmentation that occur in pregnancy and in some women taking oral contracep-tives. The mechanism for this localised increased hormonal sen-sitivity is unknown.

units.title: Hair disorders
units.summary: These can be subdivided into disorders that cause loss of hair (alopecia) or excessive hair growth (hypertrichosis and hirsutism). It can be further subdivided into localised and diffuse, and into scarring and non-scarring subtypes (Box 26.30). Alopecia can be observed in association with inflammatory disorders that cause scarring (lichen planus, discoid lupus) and others that do not cause scarring (tinea capitis, psoriasis, seborrhoeic eczema). Alopecia areata has an autoimmune basis and there is a strong genetic component, with a family history in approximately 20% of cases.

units.title: Granulomatous disease
units.summary: This is common and may be reactive, although a trigger is usually not apparent. The hallmark is the presence of dermal granulomas, which are usually palisading and associated with alteration of dermal collagen (necrobiosis). The condition is generally asymptomatic and may present as an isolated dermal lesion with a raised papular annular edge or may be more generalised. An association between generalised disease and diabetes has been proposed but not confirmed.

units.title: Porphyrias
units.summary: The porphyrias are a diverse group of diseases, caused by reduced or absent activity of specific enzymes in the porphyrin–haem biosynthetic pathway. Due to this loss of enzyme activity, porphyrin precursors prox-imal to the implicated enzyme step accumulate. If the accumulated porphyrins absorb visible light, then there will be skin features and photo-sensitivity, which explains why some porphyrias have skin features (por-phyria cutanea tarda) and others do not (acute intermittent porphyria). The most common skin presentations are photo-exposed site blistering, skin fragility and pain on daylight exposure.

units.title: Abnormal deposition disorders
units.summary: Deposits of fatty material in the skin, subcutaneous fat and tendons may be the first clue to primary or secondary hyperlipidaemia. Cutaneous amyloid may present as periocular plaques in primary sys-temic amyloidosis and amyloid associated with multiple myeloma but is uncommon in systemic amyloidosis secondary to rheumatoid arthritis or other chronic inflammatory diseases. Amyloid infiltration of blood vessels may manifest as ‘pinch purpura’ following skin trauma. Macular amyloid is more common in darker skin types and appears as pruritic grey/brown macules or patches, usually on the back.

units.title: Genetic disorders
units.summary: This condition can present with skin lesions. This is an autosomal dominant condition, and two genetic loci have been identified: TSC1 (chromosome 9) encoding hamartin, and TSC2 (chro-mosome 16) encoding tuberin. The classic triad of clinical features comprises learning disability, epilepsy and skin lesions but there is marked heterogeneity in clinical features. Skin changes include pale oval (ash leaf) macules that occur in early childhood; yellowish/pink papules in the mid-face (angiofibromas, ‘adenoma sebaceum’), occurring in adolescence; periungual and subu-ngual fibromas; and connective tissue naevi (shagreen patches, often on lower back).

The disease is likely to have an immu-nological basis. Lesions are multiple, erythematous, annular, targetoid ‘bull’s eyes’ (Fig. Extensive disease with mucosal involvement and systemic upset can sometimes occur.

Cutaneous drug reactions typically present in specific patterns (Box 26.35).

units.title: Functional anatomy and physiology
units.summary: The nervous system comprises billions of specialised cells, forming a spectacular network of connections. In addition to neurons, there are many types of glial cells. Astrocytes form the structural framework for neurons and control their biochemical environment, their foot processes adjoining small blood vessels and forming the blood–brain barrier (Fig. Oligodendrocytes are responsible for the formation and mainte-nance of the myelin sheath, which surrounds axons and is essential for maintaining the speed and consistency of action potential propagation along axons. The role of the central nervous system (CNS) is to generate outputs in response to external stimuli and changes in internal conditions.

units.title: Generation and transmission of the nervous impulse
section_path: Generation and transmission of the nervous impulse
units.summary: The role of the central nervous system (CNS) is to generate outputs in response to external stimuli and changes in internal conditions. The CNS has to maintain a delicate balance between responsivity to external stim-uli and remaining stoic enough to remain stable in a rapidly changing environment. Each neuron receives input by synaptic transmission from dendrites (branched projections of other neurons), which sum to pro-duce output in the form of an action potential that is then conducted along the axon, resulting in synaptic transmission to other neurons or, in the motor system, to muscle cells. Summation of the inputs causes net changes in the target neuron’s electrochemical gradient, which, if large enough, will trigger an action potential.

units.title: Functional anatomy of the nervous system
section_path: Functional anatomy of the nervous system
units.summary: Major components of the nervous system and their inter-relationships are depicted in Figure 27.3. The cerebral hemispheres coordinate the highest level of nervous function, the anterior half dealing with executive (‘doing’) functions and the posterior half constructing a perception of the environment. Each cerebral hemi-sphere has four functionally specialised lobes (Box 27.2 and Fig. 27.4), with some functions being distributed asymmetrically (‘lateralised’), to pro-duce cerebral dominance for functions such as motor control, speech or memory.

units.title: Localising lesions in the central nervous system
section_path: Localising lesions in the central nervous system
units.summary: After taking a history and examining the patient, the clinician should have an idea of the nature and site of any pathology (see Box 27.10). Given the intricate anatomy of the brainstem, this section will dwell on the possible localisation in more detail (see Fig. Brainstem lesions typically present with symptoms due to cranial nerve, cerebellar and upper motor neuron dysfunction and are most commonly caused by vascular disease. Since the anatomy of the brain-stem is very precisely organised, it is usually possible to localise the site of a lesion on the basis of careful history and examination in order to determine exactly which tracts/nuclei are affected, usually invoking the fewest number of lesions.

units.title: Investigation of neurological disease
units.summary: Neurological imaging has traditionally allowed only assessment of struc-ture but advances are allowing much more sophistication. Imaging modalities can use ionising radiation (plain X-rays, computed tomogra-phy (CT), CT perfusion (CTP), CT angiography, myelography and angiog-raphy), magnetic resonance (MR imaging (MRI), MR angiography (MRA)), ultrasound (Doppler imaging of blood vessels) and nuclear medicine techniques (single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) and positron emission tomography (PET)). The uses and limitations of each of these are shown in Box 27.4. Different sequences for analysing MRI signals can provide helpful information for characterising tissues and pathologies (Box 27.5). The electroencephalogram (EEG) detects electrical activity arising in the cerebral cortex via electrodes placed on the scalp to record the amplitude and frequency of the resulting waveforms.

units.title: Neurophysiological testing
units.summary: The electroencephalogram (EEG) detects electrical activity arising in the cerebral cortex via electrodes placed on the scalp to record the amplitude and frequency of the resulting waveforms. With closed eyes, the normal background activity is 8–13 Hz (known as alpha rhythm), most prominent occipitally and suppressed on eye open-ing. Other frequency bands seen over different parts of the brain in different circumstances are beta (faster than 13/sec), theta (4–8/sec) and delta (slower than 4/sec). Normal EEG patterns evolve with age and alertness; lower frequencies predominate in the very young and during sleep.

units.summary: Most headaches are chronic disorders but acute presentation of head-aches is an important aspect of emergency medical care. Headache may be divided into primary (benign) or secondary, and most patients, whether presenting in clinic or as emergencies, have primary syndromes (see Box 10.13). The emergency clinical assessment of headaches is dealt with on page 222. units.title: Dizziness, blackouts and ‘funny turns’
units.summary: Acute onset of dizziness or blackouts will present to the acute medical department. In neurological practice, it is common to deal with patients presenting with a history of multiple events. While detailed questioning will be dealt with in the relevant section (p. 221), the neurologist will have to tease out the pattern of each of the different attack types experienced by the patient to be able to form a treatment and investigation plan, one of the challenges of clinical neurology.

units.title: Status epilepticus
units.summary: Status epilepticus is seizure activity not resolving spontaneously, or recur-rent seizure with no recovery of consciousness in between. Persisting seizure activity has a recognised mortality and is a medical emergency. Diagnosis is usually clinical and can be made on the basis of the description of prolonged rigidity and/or clonic movements with loss of awareness. As seizure activity becomes prolonged, movements may become more subtle.

units.summary: In the absence of signifi-cant functional impairment (e.g. inability to work, dyspraxias, loss of daily function), many patients will prove to have benign memory dysfunction related to age, mood or psychiatric disorders. Temporary loss of memory may be due to a transient delirium related to infection, the post-ictal period after seizure, or transient global amne-sia.

units.title: Weakness
units.summary: The assessment of weakness requires the application of basic anat-omy, physiology and some pathology to the interpretation of the history and clinical findings. Points to consider are shown on Figure 27.20 and in Boxes 27.13 and 27.14. The pattern and evolution of weakness and the clinical signs provide clues to the site and nature of the lesion. It is important to establish whether the patient has loss of power rather than reduced sensation or generalised fatigue.

units.title: Sensory disturbance
units.summary: Sensory symptoms are common and frequently benign. Patients often find sensory symptoms difficult to describe and sensory examination is difficult for both doctor and patient. While neurological disease can cause sensory symptoms, systemic disorders can also be responsible. Tingling in both hands and around the mouth can occur as the result of hyperventilation or hypocalcaemia.

units.title: Abnormal movements
units.summary: Disorders of movement lead to either extra, unwanted movement (hyperki-netic disorders) or too little movement (hypokinetic disorders) (Box 27.15). In either case, the lesion often localises to the basal ganglia, although some tremors are related to cerebellar or brainstem disturbance. Functional move-ment disorders are common and may mimic all of the organic syndromes below. The most important hypokinetic disorder is Parkinson disease.

units.title: Abnormal perception
units.summary: The parietal lobes are involved in the higher processing and integration of primary sensory information. This takes place in areas referred to as ‘association’ cortex, damage to which gives rise to sensory (including visual) inattention, disorders of spatial perception and disruption of spa-tially orientated behaviour, leading to apraxias. Apraxia is the inability to perform complex, organised activity in the presence of normal basic motor, sensory and cerebellar function (after weakness, numbness and ataxia have been excluded as causes). Examples of complex motor activities include dressing, using cutlery and geographical orientation.

units.title: Altered balance and vertigo
units.summary: Balance is a complicated dynamic process that requires ongoing modi-fication of both axial and limb muscles to compensate for the effects of gravity and alterations in body position and load (and hence centre of grav-ity) in order to prevent a person from falling. This requires input from a vari-ety of sensory modalities (visual, vestibular and proprioceptive), processing by the cerebellum and brainstem, and output via a number of descending pathways (e.g. vestibulospinal, rubrospinal and reticulospinal tracts). Disorders of balance can therefore arise from any part of this pro-cess.

units.title: Abnormal gait
units.summary: Observing patients as they walk into the consulting room can be very informative, although formal examination is also important. Neurogenic gait disorders need to be distinguished from those due to skeletal abnormalities, usually char-acterised by pain producing an antalgic gait, or limp. Gait alteration incompatible with any anatomical or physiological deficit may be due to functional disorders. Upper motor neuron lesions cause characteristic extension of the affected leg.

units.title: Abnormal speech and language
units.summary: Speech disturbance may be isolated to disruption of sound output (dys-arthria) or may involve language disturbance (dysphasia). Dysphonia (reduction in the sound/volume) is usually due to mechanical laryngeal disruption, whereas dysarthria is more typically neurological in origin. Dysphasia is always neurological and localises to the dominant cerebral hemisphere (usually left, regardless of handedness). Combinations of speech and swallowing problems are explained below.

units.title: Disturbance of smell
units.summary: Symptomatic olfactory loss is most commonly due to local causes (nasal obstruction) but may follow head injury. Hyposmia may predate motor symptoms in Parkinson disease by many years, although it is rarely noticed by the patient. Positive olfactory symptoms may arise in Alzheimer disease or epilepsy.

units.title: Visual disturbance and ocular abnormalities
units.summary: Disturbances of vision may be due to primary ocular disease or to disor-ders of the central connections and visual cortex. Visual symptoms are usually negative (loss of vision) but sometimes positive, most commonly in migraine. Eye movements may be disturbed, giving rise to double vision (diplopia) or blurred vision. Loss of vision is also discussed on page 1251.

units.title: Bulbar symptoms – dysphagia and dysarthria
units.summary: Swallowing is a complex activity involving the coordinated action of lips, tongue, soft palate, pharynx and larynx, which are innervated by cranial nerves 7, 9, 10, 11 and 12. Structural causes of dysphagia are considered on page 813. Neurological mechanisms are vulnerable to damage at different points, resulting in dysphagia that is usually accom-panied by dysarthria. Tempo is again crucial: acute onset of dyspha-gia may occur as a result of brainstem stroke or a rapidly developing neuropathy, such as Guillain–Barré syndrome or diphtheria.

units.title: Bladder, bowel and sexual disturbance
units.summary: While isolated disturbances of bladder, bowel and sexual function are rarely the sole presenting features of neurological disease, they are com-mon complications of many chronic disorders such as multiple scle-rosis, stroke and dementia, and are frequently found post head injury. Abnormalities in these functions considerably reduce quality of life for patients. Incontinence and its management are discussed elsewhere (pp. The anatomy and physiology involved in controlling bladder functions are discussed in Chapter 18, but it is worth emphasising the role of the pontine micturition centre, which is itself under higher control via inputs from the pre-frontal cortex, mid-brain and hypothalamus.

units.title: Personality change
units.summary: While this is often due to psychiatric illness, neurological conditions that alter the function of the frontal lobes can cause personality change and mood disorder (see Box 27.2). Personality change due to a frontal lobe disorder may occur as the result of structural damage due to stroke, trauma, tumour or hydrocephalus. The nature of any change may help localise the lesion. Patients with mesial frontal lesions become increasingly withdrawn, unresponsive and mute (abulic), often in association with urinary incon-tinence, gait apraxia and an increase in tone known as ‘gegenhalten’ or paratonia, in which the patient varies the resistance to movement in proportion to the force exerted by the examiner.

units.title: Sleep disturbance
units.summary: Disturbances of sleep are common and are not usually due to neurological disease. Patients may complain of insomnia (difficulty sleeping), exces-sive daytime sleepiness, disturbed behaviour during night-time sleep, parasomnia (sleep walking and talking, or night terrors) or disturbing sub-jective experiences during sleep and/or its onset (nightmares, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis). A careful history (from bed partner as well as patient) usually allows specific causes of sleep disturbance to be identi-fied and these are discussed in more detail on page 1204.

units.title: Psychiatric disorders
units.summary: Psychiatric disorders may cause or result from neurological problems. Care is needed in their identification, as effective management will help the underlying neurological illness. Mood and sleep disturbance will exacerbate neurological symptoms, thus increasing disability. The best practitioners have the skill to carry the patient with them when describing the patterns of behaviour contributing to worsening symptoms.

units.title: Headache syndromes
units.summary: This is the most common type of headache and is experienced to some degree by the majority of the population. Tension-type headache is incompletely understood, and some consider that it is simply a milder version of migraine; certainly, the original notion that it is due primarily to muscle tension (hence the unsatisfactory name) has long since been dismissed. Anxiety about the headache itself may lead to continuation of symptoms, and patients may become convinced of a serious underlying condition. The pain of tension headache is characterised as ‘dull’, ‘tight’ or like a ‘pressure’, and there may be a sensation of a band round the head or pressure at the vertex. Migraine usually appears before middle age, or occasionally in later life; it affects about 20% of females and 6% of males at some point in life.

units.title: Migraine
units.summary: Migraine usually appears before middle age, or occasionally in later life; it affects about 20% of females and 6% of males at some point in life. Migraine is usually readily identifiable from the history, although unusual variants can cause uncertainty. The cause of migraine is unknown but there is increasing evidence that the aura (see below) is due to dysfunction of ion channels caus-ing a spreading front of cortical depolarisation (excitation) followed by hyperpolarisation (depression of activity). This process (the ‘spreading depression of Leão’) spreads over the cortex at a rate of about 3 mm/ min, corresponding to the aura’s symptomatic spread.

units.title: Medication overuse headache
units.summary: With increasing availability of over-the-counter medication, headache syndromes perpetuated by analgesia intake are becoming much more common. Medication overuse headache (MOH) can complicate any headache syndrome but is especially common with migraine and chronic tension-type headache. The most frequent culprits are compound anal-gesics (particularly codeine and other opiate-containing preparations) and triptans, and MOH is usually associated with use on more than 10–15 days per month. Management is by withdrawal of the responsible analgesics.

units.title: Functional neurological disorder
units.summary: Many patients present with functional symptoms and some may have a functional neurological disorder (FND). FND (also known as func-tional neurological symptom disorder, dissociative neurological symp-tom disorder, or in the past conversion disorder) is a disorder at the interface of neurology and psychiatry, reflecting function or dysfunc-tion in the shared organ, the brain. The symptoms are involuntary and cause considerable disability. Core to the assessment and man-agement of most patients is a diagnosis made on positive grounds, communicated to patients in a manner that contributes constructively to management.

units.title: Stroke
units.summary: Cerebral infarction is usually due to atherothromboembolism. The source of embolism can be the heart, particularly when there is atrial fibrillation (AF), or the rupture of large artery atherosclerosis and sub-sequent thromboembolism from carotid arteries, vertebral arteries and aortic arch. Intracranial atheroma can lead to in situ thrombosis. Occlusion of the small perforating lenticulostriate arteries in patients with sporadic or genetic small vessel diseases leads to ‘lacunar’ infarctions. Most strokes develop suddenly within a matter of minutes or hours, and are one of the differential diagnoses of patients with almost any acute focal neurological presentation.

units.title: Examination
units.summary: Rapid clinical assessment of suspected stroke is performed using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS; Box 27.28). Blood sugar, blood pressure and swallow should be checked at the bed-side. General examination should be delayed until after acute stroke treatments, like thrombolysis, have been given to eligible patients. Examination should pay attention to potential causes and any complica-tions of the stroke (Box 27.29).

units.title: Investigations

Immediate brain imag-ing is a help and sometimes essential (Box 27.34).

units.title: Management
units.summary: Nimodipine is given to prevent delayed cerebral ischaemia in the acute phase. Insertion of platinum coils into an aneurysm (via an endovascular procedure) or surgical clipping of the aneurysm neck reduces the risk of both early and late recurrent SAH. Coiling is associated with fewer perioperative complications and better outcomes than surgical clipping: where feasible, it is now the procedure of first choice. Treatment may also be needed for complications of SAH, which include obstructive hydrocephalus (that may require drainage via a shunt), delayed cerebral ischaemia due to vasospasm (which may be treated with vasodilators), hyponatraemia (best managed by fluid restriction) and systemic compli-cations associated with immobility, such as chest infection and venous thrombosis.

units.title: Cerebral venous disease
units.summary: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis usually presents with symptoms of raised intracranial pressure, seizures and focal neurological symptoms. The clinical features vary according to the sinus involved (Box 27.38 and see Fig. Cortical vein thrombosis presents with focal cortical defi-cits such as aphasia and hemiparesis (depending on the area affected), and epilepsy (focal or generalised). Occlusion of the larger veins may present with severe illness, but also with a milder illness of headache and papilloedema. MR venography demonstrates a filling defect in the affected vessel.

units.title: Epilepsy
units.summary: A seizure can be defined as the occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal, excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain. The lifetime risk of an isolated seizure is about 5%, although incidence is highest at the extremes of age. Epilepsy is the tendency to have unpro-voked seizures. While the prevalence of active epilepsy in European countries is about 0.5%, this figure varies globally and can be influenced by the prevalence of parasitic illnesses such as cysticercosis.

units.title: Vestibular disorders
units.summary: Vertigo is the typical symptom caused by vestibular dysfunction, and most patients with vertigo have acute vestibular failure, benign parox-ysmal positional vertigo or Ménière disease. Central (brain) causes of vertigo are rare by comparison, with the exception of migraine. Although commonly called ‘labyrinthitis’ or ‘vestibular neuronitis’, acute vestibular failure is a more accurate term, as most cases are idiopathic. It usually presents as isolated severe vertigo with vomiting and unstead-iness.

units.title: Disorders of sleep
units.summary: There are primary and secondary causes (Box 27.55). The most com-mon causes are impaired sleep due to lifestyle issues or sleep-disordered breathing. Sleepiness may be measured using the Epworth sleepiness scale (see Box 17.87). Most causes will be identified by a detailed history from the patient and their bed partner, and a 2-week sleep diary. Parasomnias are abnormal motor behaviours that occur around sleep.

units.title: Parasomnias
units.summary: Parasomnias are abnormal motor behaviours that occur around sleep. They may arise in either REM or non-REM sleep, with characteristic fea-tures and timing. Non-REM parasomnias tend to occur early in sleep. Parasomnias should be distinguished from other motor disturbances (such as periodic limb movements, hypnic jerks or sleep talking) and sleep-onset epileptic seizures.

units.title: Neuro-inflammatory diseases
units.summary: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an important treatable cause of long-term disability in adults. The annual incidence is around 7 per 100000, while the lifetime risk of developing MS is about 1 in 400. The incidence of MS is higher in Northern Europeans and the disease is about twice as common in females. There is evidence that both genetic and environmental factors play a causative role. The prevalence of MS is low near the equator and increases in the temperate zones of both hemispheres.

units.title: Pathophysiology
units.summary: There is evidence that both genetic and environmental factors play a causative role. The prevalence of MS is low near the equator and increases in the temperate zones of both hemispheres. People retain the risk of developing the disease in the zone in which they grew up, indicating that environmental exposures during growth and development are important. Prevalence also correlates with environmental factors, such as sunlight exposure, vitamin D and exposure to Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), although causative mechanisms remain unclear.

units.title: Clinical features
units.summary: The diagnosis of MS requires the demonstration of otherwise unex-plained CNS lesions separated in time and space (Box 27.58); tradi-tionally, this meant two or more clinical relapses affecting different parts of the nervous system, and the first ever episode is often referred to as a ‘clinically isolated syndrome’ (CIS). However, recent changes to diag-nostic criteria mean that MS may be diagnosed after an isolated episode because MRI can identify clinically silent lesions of different ages, and the presence of unpaired oligoclonal bands in the CSF can strongly suggest the development of future events (see Box 27.58). As such, MS can be proactively diagnosed and treated compared to a decade ago. The peak age of onset of MS is the fourth decade; onset in childhood or after the age of 70 years is less common but can occur.

MRI is the most sensitive technique for imaging lesions in brain and spinal cord (Fig. 27.43) and for excluding other causes that have provoked the neurological deficit.

units.title: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
units.summary: This is an acute, often severe monophasic demyelinating condition in which areas of perivenous demyelination are widely disseminated throughout the brain and spinal cord. The illness may arise spontaneously but often occurs a week or so after a viral infection, especially measles or chickenpox, or fol-lowing vaccination, suggesting that it is immunologically mediated.

units.summary: Headache, vomiting, pyrexia, delirium and meningism may be present-ing features, often with focal or multifocal brain and spinal cord signs. A minority of patients who recover have further episodes.

units.summary: MRI shows multiple high-signal areas in a pattern similar to that of MS, although often with large confluent areas of abnormality. CSF may be normal or show an increase in protein and lymphocytes (occasionally > 100×10 6 cells/L). Oligoclonal bands may be found in the acute epi-sode but, in contrast to MS, do not persist beyond clinical recovery. The clinical picture may be very similar to a first relapse of MS.

units.summary: The prognosis for acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is generally good, although occasionally it may be fatal. Treatment with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, using the same regimen as for a relapse of MS, is recommended. units.title: Paraneoplastic neurological disorders
units.summary: Neurological disease may occur with systemic malignant tumours in the absence of cerebral metastases. It is now recognised that, in the majority of these cases, antigen production in the body of the tumour leads to development of antibodies to parts of the CNS. Paraneoplastic condi-tions are increasingly recognised and the number of antibodies identified is also growing (Box 27.63). These syndromes are particularly associ-ated with small-cell carcinoma of lung, ovarian tumours and lymphomas.

units.title: Neurodegenerative diseases
units.summary: While MS is the most common cause of disability in young people in the UK, vascular and neurodegenerative diseases are increasingly important in later life. The neurodegenerative diseases are united in having a patho-logical process that leads to specific neuronal death, causing relentlessly progressive symptoms, with incidence rising with age. The causes are not yet known, although genetic influences are important. Alzheimer dis-ease and Parkinson disease are the most common.

The frequency of these varies geographically and in relation to socioeconomic level. tuberculosis and cysticercosis, may not be prevalent in the United Kingdom, they are common in other regions and therefore occur in returning travellers or immi-grants.

In low-income countries tuberculoma and other infections are frequent causes, but in the West intracranial haemorrhage and brain tumours are more common. The clinical features depend on the site of the mass, its nature and its rate of expansion. Symptoms and signs (see Box 27.87) are produced by a number of mechanisms.

units.title: Disorders of cerebellar function
units.summary: Cerebellar dysfunction can manifest as incoordination of limb function, gait ataxia, speech or eye movements. Acute dysfunction may be caused by alcohol or prescription drugs (especially the sodium channel-blocking antiseizure medications phenytoin and carbamazepine). Inflammatory changes in the cerebellum may cause symptoms in the aftermath of some infections (especially herpes zoster) or as a para-neoplastic phenomenon. The hereditary spinocerebellar ataxias are described on page 1213; they manifest as progressive ataxias in mid-dle and old age, often with other neurological features that aid specific diagnosis.

section_path: Disorders of the spine and spinal cord
units.summary: The spinal cord and spinal roots may be affected by intrinsic disease or by disorders of the surrounding meninges and bones. The clinical pres-entation of these conditions depends on the anatomical level at which the cord or roots are affected, as well as the nature of the pathological process involved. It is important to recognise when the spinal cord is at risk of compression so that urgent action can be taken.

units.title: Diseases of peripheral nerves
units.summary: Disorders of the peripheral nervous system are common and may affect the motor, sensory or autonomic components, either in isolation or in com-bination. The site of pathology may be nerve root (radiculopathy), nerve plexus (plexopathy) or nerve (neuropathy). Neuropathies may present as mononeuropathy (single nerve affected), multiple mononeuropathies (‘mononeuritis multiplex’) or a symmetrical polyneuropathy (Box 27.96). Cranial nerves 3–12 share the same tissue characteristics as peripheral nerves elsewhere and are subject to the same range of diseases.

units.title: Diseases of muscle
units.summary: Muscle disease, either hereditary or acquired, is rare. Most typically, it presents with a proximal symmetrical weakness. Diagnosis is depend-ent on recognition of clinical clues, such as cardiorespiratory involve-ment, evolution, family history, exposure to drugs, the presence of contractures, myotonia and other systemic features, and on investi-gation findings, most importantly EMG and muscle biopsy. Hereditary syndromes include the muscular dystrophies, muscle channelopathies, metabolic myopathies (including mitochondrial diseases) and congen-ital myopathies.

units.summary: A patient describes a two-day history of progressive tingling and numbness, starting in both feet but now including both arms. units.title: Medical ophthalmology
units.summary: The ability to see is an important aspect of everyday life. Although rarely a cause of mortality, visual impairment can have a profoundly negative impact on socioeconomic status, and the prevalence of blindness is dis-proportionately increased in less affluent parts of the world. Examination of the eye should be an integral part of clinical assessment. Abnormalities of the eye can be due to intrinsic ocular abnormalities or can be manifestations of systemic disease. The eyelids serve essential protective and functional roles, including shielding the eye, distributing the tear film and maintaining ocular surface integrity.

units.title: Functional anatomy and physiology
units.summary: The eyelids serve essential protective and functional roles, including shielding the eye, distributing the tear film and maintaining ocular surface integrity. Structurally, they consist of tarsal plates containing meibomian glands, the orbicularis oculi muscle (responsible for eyelid closure and innervated by the facial nerve), the levator palpebrae superioris muscle (which elevates the upper eyelid, innervated by the oculomotor nerve), and the Müller muscle (sympathetically innervated, assisting in eyelid elevation). Sensory innervation is provided by the trigeminal nerve, with the ophthalmic (V 1) and maxillary (V 2) divisions innervating the upper and lower eyelids, respectively. The eye comprises three principal layers (Fig. 28.1): the outer fibrous tunic (sclera/cornea), the middle vascular tunic (uvea), and the inner neu-ral tunic (retina), each playing distinct roles in maintaining ocular function.

units.title: Anatomy of the eye
units.summary: The eye comprises three principal layers (Fig. 28.1): the outer fibrous tunic (sclera/cornea), the middle vascular tunic (uvea), and the inner neu-ral tunic (retina), each playing distinct roles in maintaining ocular function. The sclera is a dense, avascular connective tissue providing structural integrity and serves as the attachment site for the extraocular muscles. The cornea is a transparent, avascular structure composed of six layers: the epithelium, Bowman layer, stroma, Dua layer, Descemet membrane and endothelium.

units.title: The orbit
units.summary: The orbit is a bony cavity that houses and protects the eye, along with its associated structures, including the extraocular muscles, optic nerve, blood vessels and fat. The orbital walls are formed by seven bones: the frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, lacrimal and ethmoid bones. The orbit’s primary function is to protect the eye from trauma and to provide a stable and functional environment for ocular movements. Orbital fat cushions the eye within the orbit, allowing for smooth movement and acting as a shock absorber.

units.title: Lacrimal system
units.summary: The lacrimal system plays a vital role in the production, distribution, and drainage of tears, which are essential for ocular surface health and vision. Tears provide lubrication, remove debris and contain antimicrobial pro-teins such as lysozyme. Located in the superolateral aspect of the orbit, the lacrimal gland produces the aqueous layer of the tear film. Stimulation of the lacrimal gland is primarily mediated by the para-sympathetic nervous system via the facial nerve (7th cranial nerve).

units.title: Investigation of visual disorders
units.summary: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy is a fundamental technique that allows for a detailed examination of the anterior segment of the eye, including the cornea, iris, lens and anterior chamber. To visualise the posterior seg-ment, a fundus lens is used. This allows for a non-contact stereoscopic view of the retina. Intraocular pressure (IOP) refers to the fluid pressure inside the eye, which is regulated by the balance between the production and drain-age of aqueous humour in the anterior chamber of the eye. Elevated IOP is a significant risk factor for glaucoma, a group of eye diseases that can lead to optic nerve damage and vision loss.

units.title: Intraocular pressure assessment (tonometry)
units.summary: Intraocular pressure (IOP) refers to the fluid pressure inside the eye, which is regulated by the balance between the production and drain-age of aqueous humour in the anterior chamber of the eye. Elevated IOP is a significant risk factor for glaucoma, a group of eye diseases that can lead to optic nerve damage and vision loss. The gold standard for measuring IOP is Goldmann Applanation Tonometry. This device is commonly attached on an ophthalmic slit lamp but requires a degree of clinical experience to use.

units.title: Optical coherence tomography
units.summary: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive imaging modality that provides high-resolution cross-sectional images of the retina, optic nerve and macula. It plays a critical role in diagnosing and monitoring retinal conditions such as age-related macular degeneration, diabetic macular oedema and glaucoma.

units.title: Fundus photography
units.summary: Fundus photography captures detailed images of the retina, optic disc, macula and posterior pole, allowing for documentation and longitudinal comparison of retinal changes over time. Advances in wide-field imaging technology now enable up to 200 degrees of the retina to be photo-graphed in a single image through an undilated pupil.

units.title: Fundus angiography
units.summary: Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) involves the intravenous injec-tion of fluorescein dye to visualise the retinal and choroidal vasculature. Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) uses indocyanine green dye to provide enhanced imaging of the choroidal circulation, making it particu-larly useful in diagnosing conditions like polypoidal choroidal vasculopa-thy and uveitis disorders of the choriocapillaris. OCT angiography (OCTA) is a form of OCT that provides detailed images of the blood flow in the retina and choroid without requiring dye injection. It is particularly useful for assessing macular diseases, such as wet age-related macular degeneration.

units.title: Visual field testing
units.summary: Visual field testing, such as the Humphrey automated visual field test, is used to assess both peripheral and central vision. Automated perimetry is generally superior to confrontational visual field test-ing and is considered the gold standard, as it provides a quantita-tive assessment that allows for tracking changes over time. Visual field defects are often associated with conditions like glaucoma, optic neuropathies and neurological disorders affecting the visual pathway.

units.title: B-scan ultrasound
units.summary: B-scan ultrasound allows visualisation of the posterior segment of the eye when conditions like dense cataracts or vitreous haemorrhages obstruct a direct view.

units.title: Electrophysiological tests
units.summary: Electrophysiological tests, such as electroretinography (ERG) and visual evoked potentials (VEP), assess the electrical responses of the retina and visual pathway to light stimuli, providing valuable insights into retinal and optic nerve function, especially in cases of unexplained vision loss.

units.title: Presenting problems in ophthalmic disease
units.summary: Common causes of acute red eye are summarised in Box 28.1. Differentiating the causes of acute red eye is best achieved through a slit-lamp examination, which allows for the identification of intraocular inflammation and the assessment of IOP. In the absence of a slit lamp, serious pathology can typically be identified by screening for reduced visual acuity, elevated IOP, abnormal pupil response to light and corneal pathology. Fluorescein eye drops or fluorets should be used to evaluate the integrity of the ocular surface under cobalt blue light, to detect any epithelial defects or ulcers. Sudden loss of vision is an ophthalmic emergency and should prompt urgent referral to ophthalmology for evaluation.

units.summary: Sudden loss of vision is an ophthalmic emergency and should prompt urgent referral to ophthalmology for evaluation. Clinical fundus and optic nerve appearance usually enable the diagnosis to be determined.

units.title: Gradual loss of vision
units.summary: Gradual loss in vision can be attributed to any ocular structure along the visual pathway, and common causes are summarised in Box 28.3.

units.title: Flashes and floaters
units.summary: Flashes usually result from retinal traction, such as vitreoretinal traction or proliferative retinopathies like diabetic retinopathy or sickle-cell retin-opathy. However, flashes can also have neurological causes, including migraine auras or occipital lobe disturbances, which should be consid-ered if retinal pathology is not identified. Floaters are common and often arise from degenerative changes in the vitreous, like vitreous condensations. They may also occur due to vitreous haemorrhage, which can happen with or without retinal tears.

units.title: Watery eye (epiphora)
units.summary: Epiphora, or excessive tearing, can result from three main mecha-nisms: increased tear production, impaired lacrimal pump function, or decreased tear drainage. • Reflex tearing: triggered by local irritation or inflammation, com-mon causes include foreign bodies, conjunctivitis, keratitis or blepharitis. • Systemic conditions: diseases like thyroid eye disease (Graves ophthalmopathy) can cause ocular surface irritation and increased tear production. • Dysfunction in the eyelids or orbicularis oculi muscle impairs tear drainage.

units.title: Anisocoria
units.summary: Anisocoria is a condition characterised by unequal pupil sizes, which can be a normal physiological variation or indicate an underlying neurological, ocular or systemic disorder, requiring careful evaluation to determine the cause. Figure 28.4 outlines an approach to determine the underlying cause.

units.title: Ophthalmological conditions
units.summary: Viral conjunctivitis, frequently caused by adenoviruses, presents with watery discharge, conjunctival injection and often pre-auricular lymphadenopathy. Bacterial conjunctivitis is more commonly associated with purulent dis-charge, enabling differentiation from viral causes. Bacterial conjunctivitis is commonly secondary to pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Allergic conjunctivitis presents with intense itching, tearing and bilateral involvement, often accompanied by chemosis and papillary hypertrophy of the conjunctiva. Microbial keratitis is a serious and potentially blinding condition result-ing from infection of the cornea caused by bacteria, fungi, viruses or parasites, leading to corneal ulceration and inflammation.

units.title: Microbial keratitis
units.summary: Microbial keratitis is a serious and potentially blinding condition result-ing from infection of the cornea caused by bacteria, fungi, viruses or parasites, leading to corneal ulceration and inflammation. Pathogenesis typically involves a breach in the corneal epithelium, which allows microorganisms to invade and colonise the stroma. Common risk fac-tors include contact lens wear, trauma, ocular surface disease and immunosuppression. Patients with microbial keratitis often present with acute onset of eye pain, redness, photophobia, blurred vision and discharge.

units.title: Chemical injury
units.summary: Ocular chemical injuries are serious emergencies that occur when harm-ful substances come into contact with the eye. These injuries are classi-fied into alkali and acid burns, with alkali burns being more severe due to their ability to penetrate deeper into ocular tissues. Common causative agents include alkalis such as household cleaners (sodium hydroxide, pH 14), plaster (calcium hydroxide, pH 14) and acids such as battery fluid (sulphuric acid, pH 1) and bleach (sodium hypochlorite, pH 1). Acute symptoms of chemical eye injuries include intense pain, red-ness, tearing, blurred vision and a sensation of a foreign body in the eye.

units.title: Episcleritis and scleritis
units.summary: Episcleritis and scleritis are inflammatory conditions of the eye, with epi-scleritis involving the episclera (the outermost layer) and scleritis affecting the deeper scleral tissues. Episcleritis is typically benign, presenting with mild discomfort, localised redness and no vision loss. It often affects young adults and may be idiopathic or associated with mild systemic conditions. Scleritis is more severe, characterised by intense, deep eye pain, redness with a bluish hue, photophobia and potential vision impair-ment.

Episcleritis is typically benign, presenting with mild discomfort, localised redness and no vision loss.
It often affects young adults and may be idiopathic or associated with mild systemic conditions.
Scleritis is more severe, characterised by intense, deep eye pain, redness with a bluish hue, photophobia and potential vision impair-ment.

units.title: Peripheral ulcerative keratitis
units.summary: Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) is a severe and potentially sight-threat-ening type of keratitis that involves inflammation and ulceration of the peripheral cornea. It is believed to result from immune complex deposi-tion at the limbus (the border area between the cornea and the sclera), leading to obliterative vasculitis with subsequent corneal thinning and stromal melt. It is commonly associated with systemic autoimmune dis-eases (see Ch. 25) including rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, polyarteritis nodosa, relaps-ing polychondritis and microscopic polyangiitis.

units.title: Cataract
units.summary: Cataract refers to the opacification of the crystalline lens of the eye, lead-ing to impaired vision. Cataracts are the leading cause of blindness worldwide, with preva-lence increasing significantly with age. The burden of cataract-related visual impairment is particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries, where access to surgical intervention may be limited. Age-related cataracts account for the majority of cases, although congen-ital and secondary cataracts contribute to the overall disease burden.

units.title: Age-related macular degeneration
units.summary: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is an acquired, degenerative disorder affecting the macula, primarily in adults over 50 years old. Its prevalence increases with age, making it a significant cause of vision impairment in the elderly population. AMD can be categorised into two main forms: dry (atrophic) AMD and wet (neovascular) AMD. Dry AMD, the more common form, is charac-terised by subretinal drusen deposition, which may lead to blurring and metamorphopsia.

units.title: Diabetic eye disease
units.summary: Diabetic eye disease, particularly diabetic retinopathy, is one of the most common microvascular complications of diabetes and a leading cause of blindness globally. It affects approximately one-third of indi-viduals with diabetes, with prevalence rates correlating strongly with the duration of the disease and glycaemic control. In patients with type 1 diabetes, nearly all will develop some degree of retinopathy after 20 years, while up to 60% of those with type 2 diabetes may be affected. Key risk factors include poor glycaemic control, hypertension, hyperlip-idaemia and nephropathy.

units.title: Retinal vein occlusion
units.summary: Retinal vein occlusion (RVO) is a common retinal vascular disorder and a significant cause of visual impairment. It occurs due to the blockage of retinal veins, leading to increased venous pressure, haemorrhage and retinal oedema. RVO is classified into two main types: central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), where the main retinal vein is blocked, and branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO), affecting one of its smaller branches. Both types can cause vision loss, depending on the extent and location of the occlusion.

units.title: Retinal artery occlusion
units.summary: Retinal artery occlusion is a sight-threatening condition caused by the obstruction of the central retinal artery or one of its branches, leading to sudden and severe vision loss. Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) affects the entire retina, while branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) affects a specific sector of the retina corresponding to the blocked branch. These occlusions are typically due to emboli or thrombi and are associated with cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, ath-erosclerosis and cardiac diseases. Retinal artery occlusion is an ocular emergency, as the retina’s limited tolerance to ischaemia can lead to irreversible damage within a short period.

units.title: Retinal detachment
units.summary: Retinal detachment affects approximately 1 in 10 000 people per year. It is more common in individuals over 40, with a higher prevalence in males, those with high myopia, a history of eye surgery (such as cata-ract removal) or trauma. It is also associated with conditions like lattice degeneration (an abnormally thin retina) and family history. Retinal detachment occurs when the retina separates from the underly-ing retinal pigment epithelium.

units.title: Miscellaneous retinal manifestations of multisystem disorders
section_path: Miscellaneous retinal manifestations of multisystem disorders
units.summary: Sickle-cell retinopathy is a common ocular manifestation in patients with sickle-cell disorder (p. 981), particularly those with haemoglobin SC dis-order (HbSC) or HbSβ + (sickle–beta plus thalassaemia). The condition can present with asymptomatic peripheral retinal changes or progress to vision-threatening complications. Non-proliferative changes include ‘salmon patch’ haemorrhages, refractile deposits, and ‘black sunburst’ lesions.

units.title: Uveitis
units.summary: Uveitis is an umbrella term for inflammation anywhere in the uveal tract, retina, choroid or vitreous. The inflammation can be classified based on the location within the eye: anterior, intermediate, posterior or panuveitis. It may result from autoimmune disorders, infections, trauma or exposure to toxins, and it can lead to complications like glaucoma, cataracts, or vision loss if not properly treated.

units.summary: Anterior uveitis is the most common form of uveitis, characterised by inflammation of the anterior segment of the uveal tract, including the iris and ciliary body. units.title: Intermediate uveitis
units.summary: Intermediate uveitis is a disease entity where the majority of the ocular inflammation is isolated to the vitreous cavity. While approximately a third of cases are idiopathic, multiple sclerosis and sarcoidosis are common systemic associations.

units.title: Posterior uveitis
units.summary: Posterior uveitis refers to inflammation involving the retina, choroid and optic nerve. It is the least common, but most sight-threatening form of uveitis, often resulting in significant visual impairment if not promptly identified and treated. This condition can be associated with various infectious, autoimmune or systemic diseases, and requires a thorough clinical evaluation to determine the underlying cause and guide man-agement. A comprehensive review of the forms of posterior uveitis are beyond the scope of this chapter, but notable causes are outlined below.

units.title: Endophthalmitis
units.summary: Endophthalmitis is an ocular emergency characterised by marked inflammation of the intraocular cavities, typically secondary to infection. Common clinical features include severe ocular pain, significant reduc-tion in visual acuity, redness and photophobia. On examination, there is often a marked conjunctival injection, corneal oedema and a visible hypopyon in the anterior chamber. The posterior segment may exhibit vitreous opacities, and the red reflex is usually reduced or absent.

units.title: Optic disc swelling
units.summary: Optic disc swelling can be a developmental variant of normal (pseudo-papilloedema), a manifestation of optic nerve pathology or a reflection of more widespread nerve-fibre oedema, as with retinal vein occlusion. Unilateral optic disc swelling can result from various ocular, neuro-logical and systemic conditions. Key differential diagnoses are shown in Box 28.4.

units.title: Papilloedema
units.summary: Papilloedema is the swelling of the optic disc secondary to raised intra-cranial pressure as outlined in Figure 28.8. The extent of papilloedema can be graded on the Frisén scale from 0 to 5 (Box 28.5). Patients may present with symptoms such as headaches, transient visual obscura-tions, nausea, vomiting and diplopia due to 6th nerve palsy. Visual acu-ity is typically preserved in the early stages, but prolonged or severe papilloedema can lead to progressive visual field loss and permanent vision impairment.

units.title: Giant cell arteritis
units.summary: Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis, is a chronic vasculitis primarily affecting large and medium-sized arteries, particularly the temporal arteries. Clinical features, diagnosis and management are discussed in Chapter 25. Sudden, painless monocular vision loss is a common presentation and is often due to arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AAION), which results from occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries. Visual loss in GCA is typically severe and can be permanent if the diagnosis is delayed and treatment is not promptly instituted.

units.title: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
units.summary: Non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) typically presents in adults over 50 years old with sudden, painless, monocular vision loss. This vision loss often occurs upon waking and can range from mild to severe. Visual field defects are common, most notably altitudinal defects, although other patterns can occur. Patients may report blurred vision or a dark spot in their central or peripheral vision.

units.title: Optic neuritis
units.summary: Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve that often presents with acute vision loss, usually in one eye. Patients typically experience eye pain, especially with eye movement, and vision loss that progresses over hours to days. Other common symptoms include colour vision defi-cits, such as difficulty distinguishing reds, and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) (see p. Visual field defects, such as central scoto-mas, are also common.

units.title: Ocular myasthenia gravis
units.summary: Ocular myasthenia gravis (OMG) is a subtype of myasthenia gravis (Ch. 27) that primarily affects the muscles controlling eye movements and eye-lids. It commonly presents with ptosis (drooping of one or both eyelids) and diplopia (double vision) due to weakness of the extraocular mus-cles. Symptoms may fluctuate in severity and often worsen with fatigue or sustained activity.

units.title: Optic atrophy
units.summary: Optic atrophy refers to the degeneration of optic nerve, leading to optic disc pallor visible on fundoscopy. There are many causes of optic atrophy (Box 28.6). History, examination and specific investigations may help to identify the cause. Optic neuropathy refers to damage to the optic nerve, leading to visual impairment.

units.title: Glaucoma
units.summary: Glaucoma is the second leading cause of blindness worldwide after cat-aracts. It is a group of eye disorders characterised by progressive optic nerve damage, often associated with elevated IOP. The primary types of glaucoma include primary open-angle glaucoma, angle-closure glau-coma and secondary glaucomas, each with distinct pathophysiological mechanisms.

units.title: Primary open angle glaucoma
units.summary: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is the most common form of glaucoma and a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. It predominantly affects adults over 40 years of age, with increasing prev-alence in older populations. The condition shows a higher prevalence in African and Hispanic populations compared to White Europeans, with African ancestry associated with earlier onset and more rapid progression. A family history of glaucoma, elevated IOP, myopia and systemic conditions such as hypertension and diabetes are recognised risk factors.

units.title: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
units.summary: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency charac-terised by a sudden increase in IOP due to impaired outflow of aque-ous humour through a closed or narrowed anterior chamber angle. Epidemiologically, it predominantly affects older adults, with a higher incidence in females and individuals of Asian and Inuit descent. Risk fac-tors include advancing age, hyperopia, a shallow anterior chamber and a family history of the condition. Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with rapid onset of severe ocu-lar pain, headache and decreased visual acuity, often accompanied by halos around lights.

units.title: Secondary glaucoma
units.summary: Secondary glaucomas are a group of eye conditions where increased IOP results from underlying ocular or systemic disorders, leading to optic nerve damage and vision loss. These glaucomas can arise due to various causes, including eye trauma, inflammation (like uveitis), vascular disor-ders (such as central retinal vein occlusion), medications (like glucocorti-coids) or intraocular tumours.

units.title: Tense orbit
units.summary: Recognition of a tense orbit (orbital compartment syndrome) and the need for immediate intervention can be vision-saving. Orbital injuries resulting in soft tissue oedema and retrobulbar haemorrhage within the confined bony orbit can increase intraorbital pressure, restricting blood flow and causing irreversible optic nerve injury and sight loss. Visual acuity will be reduced, but to assess this may require the opening of tense eyelids. Proptosis is often painful, with resistance to retropulsion.

units.title: Orbital cellulitis and preseptal cellulitis
units.summary: Orbital cellulitis is a serious infection of the tissues surrounding the eye within the orbit. It is often caused by bacterial spread from adjacent structures such as the sinuses. It is an ophthalmic and medical emer-gency with the potential to cause loss of vision and rarely loss of life if there is extension into adjacent intracranial structures. The infection typically spreads from the paranasal sinuses, most commonly the ethmoid sinus.

units.title: Malignancies of the eye
units.summary: Skin malignancies are discussed in detail in Chapter 26. Representing approximately 85%–90% of all eyelid cancers, basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most prevalent eyelid malignancy. It typically presents as a slow-growing, pearly nodule with rolled edges, often accompanied by ulceration. While BCC rarely metastasises, it can cause extensive local tissue destruction if not treated promptly (see Fig. Accounting for about 5%–10% of eyelid malignancies, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is more aggressive than BCC.

It presents as a scaly, erythematous lesion with irregular borders and may ulcerate. Unlike BCC, SCC has a higher risk of metastasis to regional lymph nodes and distant organs.

units.title: Sebaceous carcinoma
units.summary: A rare but highly aggressive eyelid malignancy, sebaceous carcinoma arises from the sebaceous glands, commonly in the upper eyelid. It may mimic benign lesions, such as chalazia or blepharitis, causing diagnostic delays. Sebaceous carcinoma has a high recurrence rate and potential for both local invasion and distant metastasis.

units.title: Melanoma

It often presents as a pigmented lesion with irregular borders and rapid growth, requiring prompt diagnosis and management (Fig. Common risk factors for these malignancies include prolonged ultra-violet (UV) exposure, fair skin, advanced age and a history of previous skin cancers.

units.title: Ocular surface malignancies
units.summary: Malignancies of the ocular surface are rare but serious conditions that can affect the conjunctiva, cornea and surrounding tissues. The most common types include squamous cell carcinoma, conjunctival mela-noma and lymphoma. Squamous cell carcinoma typically arises from the limbal region and is associated with risk factors such as ultraviolet (UV) radiation, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and immunosuppression (Fig. Conjunctival melanoma originates from melanocytes and presents as a pigmented lesion, often associated with primary acquired melanosis (PAM).

units.title: Choroidal melanomas
units.summary: Choroidal melanomas are primary ocular malignancies originating from melanocytes. Choroidal melanoma, the most common intraocular mela-noma in adults, often presents asymptomatically but may cause blurred vision, floaters, or flashes. It appears as a pigmented or non-pigmented, dome- or mushroom-shaped lesion with possible subretinal fluid and ret-inal detachment. The diagnosis is mainly clinical through examination combined with ret-inal imaging and ultrasonography to assess the internal characteristics.

units.title: Ocular metastasis
units.summary: Ocular metastasis refers to the spread of cancer cells to the eye from a primary tumour located elsewhere in the body, most commonly originating from the breast or lung. The choroid is the most frequent site of metastasis within the eye due to its rich vascular supply. Retro-orbital locations may cause proptosis and restricted eye movements. Choroidal lesions may cause blurred vision, visual field defects or pain, although some cases are asymptomatic.

units.title: Retinoblastoma
units.summary: Retinoblastoma is the most common malignant intraocular tumour in chil-dren, originating from the retinal cells of the eye. It is primarily caused by mutations in the RB1 gene, either inherited or occurring spontaneously. The disease often presents in children under 5 years of age, with symp-toms including leucocoria (white pupillary reflex), strabismus, vision loss, or eye redness and swelling. Early diagnosis is critical and is typically made through fundoscopy, ultrasound and MRI.
